entries.22846beb2708f3d89c5b96afe0ab3943bada7f12: <div sID="gen27913" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="John.13" sID="John.13"/> <div eID="gen27913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27914" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27915" type="x-p"/> Our Saviour having finished his public discourses, in which he "endured the contradiction of sinners," now applies himself to a private conversation with his friends, in which he designed the consolation of saints. Henceforward we have an account of what passed between him and his disciples, who were to be entrusted with the affairs of his household, when he was gone into a far country; the necessary instructions and comforts he furnished them with. His hour being at hand, he applies himself to set his house in order. In this chapter I. He washes his disciples' feet, <reference osisRef="John.13.1-John.13.17">ver. 1-17</reference>. II. He foretels who should betray him, <reference osisRef="John.13.18-John.13.30">ver. 18-30</reference>. III. He instructs them in the great doctrine of his own death, and the great duty of brotherly love, <reference osisRef="John.13.31-John.13.35">ver. 31-35</reference>. IV. He foretels Peter's denying him, <reference osisRef="John.13.36-John.13.38">ver. 36-38</reference>.
entries.04b89be8d561000e4ce9dc2cac300f9e50fff01c: <div eID="gen27915" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27914" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Washing the Disciples' Feet; Necessity of Obedience.</title> <div sID="gen27916" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end. <hi type="super">2</hi> And supper being ended, the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's <hi type="italic">son,</hi> to betray him; <hi type="super">3</hi> Jesus knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he was come from God, and went to God; <hi type="super">4</hi> He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself. <hi type="super">5</hi> After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe <hi type="italic">them</hi> with the towel wherewith he was girded. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then cometh he to Simon Peter: and Peter saith unto him, Lord, dost thou wash my feet? <hi type="super">7</hi> Jesus answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter. <hi type="super">8</hi> Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me. <hi type="super">9</hi> Simon Peter saith unto him, Lord, not my feet only, but also <hi type="italic">my</hi> hands and <hi type="italic">my</hi> head. <hi type="super">10</hi> Jesus saith to him, He that is washed needeth not save to wash <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet, but is clean every whit: and ye are clean, but not all. 11 For he knew who should betray him; therefore said he, Ye are not all clean. <hi type="super">12</hi> So after he had washed their feet, and had taken his garments, and was set down again, he said unto them, Know ye what I have done to you? <hi type="super">13</hi> Ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for <hi type="italic">so</hi> I am. <hi type="super">14</hi> If I then, <hi type="italic">your</hi> Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet. <hi type="super">15</hi> For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you. <hi type="super">16</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord; neither he that is sent greater than he that sent him. <hi type="super">17</hi> If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them. <div eID="gen27916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27917" type="x-p"/> It has generally been taken for granted by commentators that Christ's washing his disciples' feet, and the discourse that followed it, were the same night in which he was betrayed, and at the same sitting wherein he ate the passover and instituted the Lord's supper; but whether before the solemnity began, or after it was all over, or between the eating of the passover and the institution of the Lord's supper, they are not agreed. This evangelist, making it his business to gather up those passages which the others had omitted, industriously omits those which the others had recorded, which occasions some difficulty in putting them together. If it was then, we suppose that <hi type="italic">Judas went out</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.13.30">v. 30</reference>) to get his men ready that were to apprehend the Lord Jesus in the garden. But Dr. Lightfoot is clearly of opinion that this was done and said, even all that is recorded to the end of <reference osisRef="John.3.31-John.14.33">ch. xiv.</reference>, not at the passover supper, for it is here said (<reference osisRef="John.13.1">v. 1</reference>) to be <hi type="italic">before the feast of the passover,</hi> but at the supper in Bethany, two days before the passover (of which we read <reference osisRef="Matt.26.2-Matt.26.6">Matt. xxvi. 2-6</reference>), at which Mary the second time anointed Christ's head with the remainder of her box of ointment. Or, it might be at some other supper the night before the passover, not as that was in the house of Simon the leper, but in his own lodgings, where he had none but his disciples about him, and could be more free with them. <div eID="gen27917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27918" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="John.13.1-John.13.17">these verses</reference> we have the story of Christ's washing his disciples' feet; it was an action of a singular nature; no miracle, unless we call it a miracle of humility. Mary had just anointed his head; now, lest his acceptance of this should look like taking state, he presently balances it with this act of abasement. But why would Christ do this? If the disciples' feet needed washing, they could wash them themselves; a wise man will not do a thing that looks odd and unusual, but for very good causes and considerations. We are sure that it was not in a humour or a frolic that this was done; no, the transaction was very solemn, and carried on with a great deal of seriousness; and four reasons are here intimated why Christ did this:—1. That he might testify his love to his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.13.1-John.13.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. 2. That he might give an instance of his own voluntary humility and condescension, <reference osisRef="John.13.3-John.13.5">v. 3-5</reference>. 3. That he might signify to them spiritual washing, which is referred to in his discourse with Peter, <reference osisRef="John.13.6-John.13.11">v. 6-11</reference>. 4. That he might set them an example, <reference osisRef="John.13.12-John.13.17">v. 12-17</reference>. And the opening of these four reasons will take in the exposition of the whole story. <div eID="gen27918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27919" type="x-p"/> I. Christ washed his disciples' feet that he might give a proof of that great love wherewith he loved them; loved them to the end, <reference osisRef="John.13.1-John.13.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen27919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27920" type="x-p"/> 1. It is here laid down as an undoubted truth that our Lord Jesus, <hi type="italic">having loved his own that were in the world, loved them to the end,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.13.1">v. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen27920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27921" type="x-p"/> (1.) This is true of the disciples that were his immediate followers, in particular the twelve. These were his own in the world, his family, his school, his bosom-friends. Children he had none to call his own, but he adopted them, and took them as his own. He had those that were his own in the other world, but he left them for a time, to look after his own in this world. These he loved, he called them into fellowship with himself, conversed familiarly with them, was always tender of them, and of their comfort and reputation. He allowed them to be very free with him, and bore with their infirmities. He loved them to the end, continued his love to them as long as he lived, and after his resurrection; he never took away his loving kindness. Though there were some persons of quality that espoused his cause, he did not lay aside his old friends, to make room for new ones, but still stuck to his poor fishermen. They were weak and defective in knowledge and grace, dull and forgetful; and yet, though he reproved them often, he never ceased to love them and take care of them. <div eID="gen27921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27922" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is true of all believers, for these twelve patriarchs were the representatives of all the tribes of God's spiritual Israel. Note, [1.] Our Lord Jesus has a people in the world that are his own,—his own, for they were given him by the Father, he has purchased them, and paid dearly for them, and he has set them apart for himself,—his own, for they have devoted themselves to him as a peculiar people. <hi type="italic">His own;</hi> where <hi type="italic">his own</hi> were spoken of that <hi type="italic">received him not,</hi> it is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tous idious</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">his own persons,</hi> as a man's wife and children are his own, to whom he stands in a constant relation. [2.] Christ has a cordial love for his own that are in the world. He <hi type="italic">did</hi> love them with a love of goodwill when he gave himself for their redemption. He <hi type="italic">does</hi> love them with a love of complacency when he admits them into communion with himself. Though they are <hi type="italic">in this world,</hi> a world of darkness and distance, of sin and corruption, yet he loves them. He was now going to his own in heaven, the spirits of just men made perfect there; but he seems most concerned for his own on earth, because they most needed his care: the sickly child is most indulged. [3.] Those whom Christ loves <hi type="italic">he loves to the end;</hi> he is constant in his love to his people; he <hi type="italic">rests in his love.</hi> He loves with an everlasting love (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer. xxxi. 3</reference>), from everlasting in the counsels of it to everlasting in the consequences of it. Nothing can separate a believer <hi type="italic">from the love of Christ;</hi> he loves his own, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eis telos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">unto perfection,</hi> for he will perfect what concerns them, will bring them to that world where love is perfect. <div eID="gen27922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27923" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ manifested his love to them by washing their feet, as that good woman (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.38">Luke vii. 38</reference>) showed her love to Christ by washing his feet and wiping them. Thus he would show that as his love to them was constant so it was condescending,—that in prosecution of the designs of it he was willing to humble himself,—and that the glories of his exalted state, which he was now entering upon, should be no obstruction at all to the favour he bore to his chosen; and thus he would confirm the promise he had made to all the saints that he would <hi type="italic">make them sit down to meat, and would come forth and serve them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.37">Luke xii. 37</reference>), would put honour upon them as great and surprising as for a lord to serve his servants. The disciples had just now betrayed the weakness of their love to him, in grudging the ointment that was poured upon his head (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.8">Matt. xxvi. 8</reference>), yet he presently gives this proof of his love to them. Our infirmities are foils to Christ's kindnesses, and set them off. <div eID="gen27923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27924" type="x-p"/> 3. He chose this time to do it, a little before his last passover, for two reasons:— <div eID="gen27924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27925" type="x-p"/> (1.) Because now <hi type="italic">he knew that his hour was come,</hi> which he had long expected, <hi type="italic">when he should depart out of this world to the Father.</hi> Observe here, [1.] The change that was to pass over our Lord Jesus; he must <hi type="italic">depart.</hi> This began at his death, but was completed at his ascension. As Christ himself, so all believers, by virtue of their union with him, when they depart out of the world, are absent from the body, <hi type="italic">go to the Father,</hi> are present with the Lord. It is a departure <hi type="italic">out of the world,</hi> this unkind, injurious world, this faithless, treacherous world—this world of labour, toil, and temptation—this vale of tears; and it is a going <hi type="italic">to the Father,</hi> to the vision of the Father of spirits, and the fruition of him as ours. [2.] The time of this change: <hi type="italic">His hour was come.</hi> It is sometimes called his enemies' hour (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.53">Luke xxii. 53</reference>), the hour of their triumph; sometimes his hour, the hour of his triumph, the hour he had had in his eye all along. The time of his sufferings was fixed to an hour, and the continuance of them but for an hour. [3.] His foresight of it: He <hi type="italic">knew that his hour was come;</hi> he knew from the beginning that it would come, and when, but now he knew that it <hi type="italic">was come.</hi> We know not when our hour will come, and therefore what we have to do in habitual preparation for it ought never to be undone; but, when we know by the harbingers that our hour is come, we must vigorously apply ourselves to an actual preparation, as our Master did, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">2 Pet. iii. 14</reference>. Now it was in the immediate foresight of his departure that he <hi type="italic">washed his disciples' feet;</hi> that, as his own head was anointed just now <hi type="italic">against the day of his burial,</hi> so their feet might be washed against the day of their consecration by the descent of the Holy Ghost fifty days after, as the priests were washed, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.6">Lev. viii. 6</reference>. When we see our day approaching, we should do what good we can to those we leave behind. <div eID="gen27925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27926" type="x-p"/> (2.) Because the <hi type="italic">devil had now put it into the heart of Judas to betray him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.13.2">v. 2</reference>. These words in a parenthesis may be considered, [1.] As tracing Judas's treason to its origin; it was a sin of such a nature that it evidently bore the devil's image and superscription. What way of access the devil has to men's hearts, and by what methods he darts in his suggestions, and mingles them undiscerned with those thoughts which are the natives of the heart, we cannot tell. But there are some sins in their own nature so exceedingly sinful, and to which there is so little temptation from the world and the flesh, that it is plain Satan lays the egg of them in a heart disposed to be the nest to hatch them in. For Judas to betray such a master, to betray him so cheaply and upon no provocation, was such downright enmity to God as could not be forged but by Satan himself, who thereby thought to ruin the Redeemer's kingdom, but did in fact ruin his own. [2.] As intimating a reason why Christ now washed his disciples' feet. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Judas being now resolved to betray him, the time of his departure could not be far off; if this matter be determined, it is easy to infer with St. Paul, <hi type="italic">I am now ready to be offered.</hi> Note, The more malicious we perceive our enemies to be against us, the more industrious we should be to prepare for the worst that may come. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Judas being now got into the snare, and the devil aiming at Peter and the rest of them (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.31">Luke xxii. 31</reference>), Christ would fortify his own against him. If the wolf has seized one of the flock, it is time for the shepherd to look well to the rest. Antidotes must be stirring, when the infection is begun. Dr. Lightfoot observes that the disciples had learned of Judas to murmur at the anointing of Christ; compare <reference osisRef="John.12.4">ch. xii. 4,</reference> and <reference osisRef="Matt.26.8">with Matt. xxvi. 8</reference>. Now, lest those that had learned that of him should learn worse, he fortifies them by a lesson of humility against his most dangerous assaults. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Judas, who was now plotting to betray him, was <hi type="italic">one of the twelve.</hi> Now Christ would hereby show that he did not design to cast them all off for the faults of one. Though one of their college had a devil, and was a traitor, yet they should fare never the worse for that. Christ loves his church though there are hypocrites in it, and had still a kindness for his disciples though there was a Judas among them and he knew it. <div eID="gen27926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27927" type="x-p"/> II. Christ washed his disciples' feet that he might give an instance of his own wonderful humility, and show how lowly and condescending he was, and let all the world know how low he could stoop in love to his own. This is intimated, <reference osisRef="John.13.3-John.13.5">v. 3-5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Jesus knowing,</hi> and now actually considering, and perhaps discoursing of, his honours as Mediator, and telling his friends that <hi type="italic">the Father had given all things into his hand, rises from supper,</hi> and, to the great surprise of the company, who wondered what he was going to do, <hi type="italic">washed his disciples' feet.</hi> <div eID="gen27927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27928" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is the rightful advancement of the Lord Jesus. Glorious things are here said of Christ as Mediator. <div eID="gen27928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27929" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">The Father had given all things into his hands;</hi> had given him a propriety in all, and a power over all, as possessor of heaven and earth, in pursuance of the great designs of his undertaking; see <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">Matt. xi. 27</reference>. The accommodation and arbitration of all matters in variance between God and man were committed into his hands as the great umpire and referee; and the administration of the kingdom of God among men, in all the branches of it, was committed to him; so that all acts, both of government and judgment, were to pass through his hands; he is <hi type="italic">heir of all things.</hi> <div eID="gen27929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27930" type="x-p"/> (2.) He <hi type="italic">came from God.</hi> This implies that he was in the beginning with God, and had a being and glory, not only before he was born into this world, but before the world itself was born; and that when he came into the world he came as God's ambassador, with a commission from him. He came from God as the son of God, and the sent of God. The Old-Testament prophets were raised up and employed for God, but Christ came directly from him. <div eID="gen27930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27931" type="x-p"/> (3.) He <hi type="italic">went to God,</hi> to be glorified with him with the same glory which he had with God from eternity. That which comes from God shall go to God; those that are born from heaven are bound for heaven. As Christ came from God to be an agent for him on earth, so he went to God to be an agent for us in heaven; and it is a comfort to us to think how welcome he was there: he was brought near to the <hi type="italic">Ancient of days,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan. vii. 13</reference>. And it was said to him, <hi type="italic">Sit thou at my right hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen27931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27932" type="x-p"/> (4.) He <hi type="italic">knew</hi> all this; was not like a prince in the cradle, that knows nothing of the honour he is born to, or like Moses, who <hi type="italic">wist not that his face shone;</hi> no, he had a full view of all the honours of his exalted state, and yet stooped thus low. But how does this come in here? [1.] As an inducement to him now quickly to leave what lessons and legacies he had to leave to his disciples, because his hour was now come when he must take his leave of them, and be exalted above that familiar converse which he now had with them, <reference osisRef="John.13.1">v. 1</reference>. [2.] It may come in as that which supported him under his sufferings, and carried him cheerfully through this sharp encounter. Judas was now betraying him, and he knew it, and knew what would be the consequence of it; yet, knowing also <hi type="italic">that he came from God and went to God,</hi> he did not draw back, but went on cheerfully. [3.] It seems to come in as a foil to his condescension, to make it the more admirable. The reasons of divine grace are sometimes represented in scripture as strange and surprising (as <reference osisRef="Isa.57.17-Isa.57.18">Isa. lvii. 17, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.13-Hos.2.14">Hos. ii. 13, 14</reference>); so here, that is given as an inducement to Christ to stoop which should rather have been a reason for his taking state; for God's thoughts are not as ours. Compare with this those passages which preface the most signal instances of condescending grace with the displays of divine glory, as <reference osisRef="Ps.68.4-Ps.68.5">Ps. lxviii. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa. lvii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1-Isa.66.2">lxvi. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen27932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27933" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is the voluntary abasement of our Lord Jesus notwithstanding this. <hi type="italic">Jesus knowing</hi> his own glory as God, and his own authority and power as Mediator, one would think it should follow, <hi type="italic">He rises from supper,</hi> lays aside his ordinary garments, calls for robes, bids them keep their distance, and do him homage; but no, quite the contrary, when he considered this he gave the greatest instance of humility. Note, A well-grounded assurance of heaven and happiness, instead of puffing a man up with pride, will make and keep him very humble. Those that would be found conformable to Christ, and partakers of his Spirit, must study to keep their minds low in the midst of the greatest advancements. Now that which Christ humbled himself to was to <hi type="italic">wash his disciples' feet.</hi> <div eID="gen27933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27934" type="x-p"/> (1.) The action itself was mean and servile, and that which servants of the lowest rank were employed in. <hi type="italic">Let thine handmaid</hi> (saith Abigail) <hi type="italic">be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord;</hi> let me be in the meanest employment, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.41">1 Sam. xxv. 41</reference>. If he had washed their hands or faces, it had been great condescension (Elisha poured water on the hands of Elijah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.11">2 Kings iii. 11</reference>); but for Christ to stoop to such a piece of drudgery as this may well excite our admiration. Thus he would teach us to think nothing below us wherein we may be serviceable to God's glory and the good of our brethren. <div eID="gen27934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27935" type="x-p"/> (2.) The condescension was so much the greater that he did this for his own disciples, who in themselves were of a low and despicable condition, not curious about their bodies; their feet, it is likely, were seldom washed, and therefore very dirty. In relation to him, they were his scholars, his servants, and such as should have washed his feet, whose dependence was upon him, and their expectations from him. Many of great spirits otherwise will do a mean thing to curry favour with their superiors; they rise by stooping, and climb by cringing; but for Christ to do this to <hi type="italic">his disciples</hi> could be no act of policy nor complaisance, but pure humility. <div eID="gen27935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27936" type="x-p"/> (3.) He <hi type="italic">rose from supper</hi> to do it. Though we translate it (<reference osisRef="John.13.2">v. 2</reference>) <hi type="italic">supper being ended,</hi> it might be better read, <hi type="italic">there being a supper made,</hi> or <hi type="italic">he being at supper,</hi> for he sat down again (<reference osisRef="John.13.12">v. 12</reference>), and we find him dipping a sop (<reference osisRef="John.13.26">v. 26</reference>), so that he did it in the midst of his meal, and thereby taught us, [1.] Not to reckon it a disturbance, nor any just cause of uneasiness, to be called from our meal to do God or our brother any real service, esteeming the discharge of our duty <hi type="italic">more than our necessary food,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.34">ch. iv. 34</reference>. Christ would not leave his preaching to oblige his nearest relations (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.33">Mark iii. 33</reference>), but would leave his supper to show his love to his disciples. [2.] Not to be over nice about our meat. It would have turned many a squeamish stomach to wash dirty feet at supper-time; but Christ did it, not that we might learn to be rude and slovenly (cleanliness and godliness will do well together), but to teach us not to be curious, not to indulge, but mortify, the delicacy of the appetite, giving good manners their due place, and no more. <div eID="gen27936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27937" type="x-p"/> (4.) He put himself into the garb of a servant, to do it: he <hi type="italic">laid aside</hi> his loose and upper <hi type="italic">garments,</hi> that he might apply himself to this service the more expeditely. We must address ourselves to duty as those that are resolved not to take state, but to take pains; we must divest ourselves of every thing that would either feed our pride or hang in our way and hinder us in what we have to do, must <hi type="italic">gird up the loins of our mind,</hi> as those that in earnest buckle to business. <div eID="gen27937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27938" type="x-p"/> (5.) He did it with all the humble ceremony that could be, went through all the parts of the service distinctly, and passed by none of them; he did it as if he had been used thus to serve; did it himself alone, and had none to minister to him in it. He <hi type="italic">girded himself with the towel,</hi> as servants throw a napkin on their arm, or put an apron before them; he <hi type="italic">poured water into the basin</hi> out of the water-pots that stood by (<reference osisRef="John.2.6">ch. ii. 6</reference>), and then <hi type="italic">washed their feet;</hi> and, to complete the service, <hi type="italic">wiped them.</hi> Some think that he did not wash the feet of them all, but only four or five of them, that being thought sufficient to answer the end; but I see nothing to countenance this conjecture, for in other places where he did make a difference it is taken notice of; and his washing the feet of them <hi type="italic">all,</hi> without exception, teaches us a catholic and extensive charity to all Christ's disciples, even the least. <div eID="gen27938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27939" type="x-p"/> (6.) Nothing appears to the contrary but that he washed the feet of Judas among the rest, for he was present, <reference osisRef="John.13.26">v. 26</reference>. It is the character of a <hi type="italic">widow indeed</hi> that she had washed the saints' feet (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10">1 Tim. v. 10</reference>), and there is some comfort in this; but the blessed Jesus here washed the feet of a sinner, the worst of sinners, the worst to him, who was at this time contriving to betray him. <div eID="gen27939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27940" type="x-p"/> Many interpreters consider Christ's washing his disciples' feet as a representation of <hi type="italic">his whole undertaking.</hi> He knew that he was equal with God, and all things were his; and yet he rose from his table in glory, laid aside his robes of light, girded himself with our nature, took upon him the form of a servant, <hi type="italic">came not to be ministered to, but to minister,</hi> poured out his blood, poured out his soul unto death, and thereby prepared a laver to wash us from our sins, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Rev. i. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen27940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27941" type="x-p"/> III. Christ washed his disciples' feet that he might signify to them spiritual washing, and the cleansing of the soul from the pollutions of sin. This is plainly intimated in his discourse with Peter upon it, <reference osisRef="John.13.6-John.13.11">v. 6-11</reference>, in which we may observe, <div eID="gen27941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27942" type="x-p"/> 1. The surprise Peter was in when he saw his Master go about this mean service (<reference osisRef="John.13.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then cometh he to Simon Peter,</hi> with his towel and basin, and bids him put out his feet to be washed. Chrysostom conjectures that he first washed the feet of Judas, who readily admitted the honour, and was pleased to see his Master so disparage himself. It is most probable that when he <hi type="italic">went about</hi> this service (which is all that is meant by his <hi type="italic">beginning</hi> to wash, <reference osisRef="John.13.5">v. 5</reference>) he took Peter first, and that the rest would not have suffered it, if they had not first heard it explained in what passed between Christ and Peter. Whether Christ came first to Peter or no, when he did come to him, Peter was startled at the proposal: <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> (saith he) <hi type="italic">dost thou wash my feet?</hi> Here is an emphasis to be laid upon the persons, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> and <hi type="italic">me;</hi> and the placing of the words is observable, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">sy mou</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">what, thou mine? Tu mihi lavas pedes? Quid est tu? Quid est mihi? Cogitanda sunt potius quam dicenda—Dost thou wash my feet? What is it thou? What to me? These things are rather to be contemplated than uttered.</hi>—Aug. in loc. What <hi type="italic">thou,</hi> our Lord and Master, whom we know and believe to be the Son of God, and Saviour and ruler of the world, do this for <hi type="italic">me,</hi> a worthless worm of the earth, <hi type="italic">a sinful man, O Lord?</hi> Shall those hands wash my feet which with a touch have cleansed lepers, given sight to the blind, and raised the dead? So Theophylact, and from him Dr. Taylor. Very willingly would Peter have taken the basin and towel, and washed his Master's feet, and been proud of the honour, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.7-Luke.17.8">Luke xvii. 7, 8</reference>. "This had been natural and regular; for <hi type="italic">my Master</hi> to wash my feet is such a solecism as never was; such a paradox as I cannot understand. <hi type="italic">Is this the manner of men?</hi>" Note, Christ's condescensions, especially his condescensions to <hi type="italic">us,</hi> wherein we find ourselves taken notice of by his grace, are justly the matter of our admiration, <reference osisRef="John.14.22">ch. xiv. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who am I, Lord God? And what is my father's house?</hi> <div eID="gen27942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27943" type="x-p"/> 2. The immediate satisfaction Christ gave to this question of surprise. This was at least sufficient to silence his objections (<reference osisRef="John.13.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">What I do, thou knowest not now, but thou shalt know hereafter.</hi> Here are two reasons why Peter must submit to what Christ was doing:— <div eID="gen27943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27944" type="x-p"/> (1.) Because he was at present in the dark concerning it, and ought not to oppose what he did not understand, but acquiesce in the will and wisdom of one who could give a good reason for all he said and did. Christ would teach Peter an <hi type="italic">implicit obedience: "What I do thou knowest not now,</hi> and therefore art no competent judge of it, but must believe it is well done because I do it." Note, Consciousness to ourselves of the darkness we labour under, and our inability to judge of what God does, should make us sparing and modest in our censures of his proceedings; see <reference osisRef="Heb.11.8">Heb. xi. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen27944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27945" type="x-p"/> (2.) Because there was something considerable in it, of which he should hereafter know the meaning: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt know hereafter</hi> what need thou hast of being washed, when thou shalt be guilty of the heinous sin of denying me;" so some. "Thou shalt know, when, in the discharge of the office of an apostle, thou wilt be employed in washing off from those under thy charge the sins and defilements of their earthly affections;" so Dr. Hammond. Note, [1.] Our Lord Jesus does many things the meaning of which even his own disciples do not for the present know, but they <hi type="italic">shall know afterwards.</hi> What he did when he became man for us and what he did when he became a worm and no man for us, what he did when he lived our life and what he did when he laid it down, could not be understood till afterwards, and then it appeared that <hi type="italic">it behoved him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.17">Heb. ii. 17</reference>. Subsequent providences explain preceding ones; and we see afterwards what was the kind tendency of events that seemed most cross; and the way which we thought was <hi type="italic">about</hi> proved the <hi type="italic">right way.</hi> [2.] Christ's washing his disciples' feet had a significancy in it, which they themselves did not understand till afterwards, when Christ explained it to be a specimen of the laver of regeneration, and till the Spirit was poured out upon them from on high. We must let Christ take his own way, both in ordinances and providences, and we shall find in the issue it was the best way. <div eID="gen27945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27946" type="x-p"/> 3. Peter's peremptory refusal, notwithstanding this, to let Christ wash his feet (<reference osisRef="John.13.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou shalt by no means wash my feet; no, never.</hi> So it is in the original. It is the language of a fixed resolution. Now, (1.) Here was a show of humility and modesty. Peter herein seemed to have, and no doubt he really had, a great respect for his Master, as he had, <reference osisRef="Luke.5.8">Luke v. 8</reference>. Thus many are beguiled of their reward in a <hi type="italic">voluntary humility</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col. ii. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.2.23">23</reference>), such a self-denial as Christ neither appoints nor accepts; for, (2.) Under this show of humility there was a real contradiction to the will of the Lord Jesus: "I <hi type="italic">will wash thy feet,</hi>" saith Christ; "But thou never shalt," saith Peter, "it is not a fitting thing;" so making himself wiser than Christ. It is not humility, but infidelity, to put away the offers of the gospel, as if too rich to be made to us or too good news to be true. <div eID="gen27946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27947" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ's insisting upon his offer, and a good reason given to Peter why he should accept it: <hi type="italic">If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.</hi> This may be taken, (1.) As a severe caution against disobedience: "<hi type="italic">If I wash thee not,</hi> if thou continue refractory, and wilt not comply with thy Master's will in so small a matter, thou shalt not be owned as one of my disciples, but be justly discarded and cashiered for not observing orders." Thus several of the ancients understand it; if Peter will make himself wiser than his Master, and dispute the commands he ought to obey, he does in effect renounce his allegiance, and say, as they did, <hi type="italic">What portion have we in David,</hi> in the Son of David? And so shall his doom be, he shall have no part in him. Let him use no more manners than will do him good, for <hi type="italic">to obey is better than sacrifice,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1 Sam. xv. 22</reference>. Or, (2.) As a declaration of the necessity of spiritual washing; and so I think it is to be understood: "<hi type="italic">If I wash not</hi> thy soul from the pollution of sin, <hi type="italic">thou hast no part with me,</hi> no interest in me, no communion with me, no benefit by me." Note, All those, and those only, that are spiritually washed by Christ, have a part in Christ. [1.] To have a part in Christ, or with Christ, has all the happiness of a Christian bound up in it, to be <hi type="italic">partakers of Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.14">Heb. iii. 14</reference>), to share in those inestimable privileges which result from a union with him and relation to him. It is that <hi type="italic">good part</hi> the having of which is the <hi type="italic">one thing needful.</hi> [2.] It is necessary to our having a part in Christ that he wash us. All those whom Christ owns and saves he justifies and sanctifies, and both are included in his washing them. We cannot partake of his glory if we partake not of his merit and righteousness, and of his Spirit and grace. <div eID="gen27947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27948" type="x-p"/> 5. Peter's more than submission, his earnest request, to be washed by Christ, <reference osisRef="John.13.9">v. 9</reference>. If this be the meaning of it, <hi type="italic">Lord, wash not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.</hi> How soon is Peter's mind changed! When the mistake of his understanding was rectified, the corrupt resolution of his will was soon altered. Let us therefore not be peremptory in any resolve (except in our resolve to follow Christ), because we may soon see cause to retract it, but cautious in taking up a purpose we will be tenacious of. Observe, <div eID="gen27948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27949" type="x-p"/> (1.) How ready Peter is to recede from what he had said: "Lord, what a fool was I to speak such a hasty word!" Now that the washing of him appeared to be an act of Christ's authority and grace he admits it; but disliked when it seemed only an act of humiliation. Note, [1.] Good men, when they see their error, will not be loth to recant it. [2.] Sooner or later, Christ will bring all to be of his mind. <div eID="gen27949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27950" type="x-p"/> (2.) How importunate he is for the purifying grace of the Lord Jesus, and the universal influence of it, even upon his hands and head. Note, A divorce from Christ, and an exclusion from having a part in him, is the most formidable evil in the eyes of all that are enlightened, for the fear of which they will be persuaded to any thing. And for fear of this we should be earnest with God in prayer, that he will wash us, will justify and sanctify us. "Lord, that I may not be cut off from thee, make me fit for thee, by the washing of regeneration. <hi type="italic">Lord, wash not my feet only</hi> from the gross pollutions that cleave to them, <hi type="italic">but also my hands and my head</hi> from the spots which they have contracted, and the undiscerned filth which proceeds by perspiration from the body itself." Note, Those who truly desire to be sanctified desire to be sanctified throughout, and to have the whole man, with all its parts and powers, purified, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1 Thess. v. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen27950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27951" type="x-p"/> 6. Christ's further explication of this sign, as it represented spiritual washing. <div eID="gen27951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27952" type="x-p"/> (1.) With reference to his disciples that were faithful to him (<reference osisRef="John.13.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that is washed</hi> all over in the bath (as was frequently practised in those countries), when he returns to his house, <hi type="italic">needeth not save to wash his feet,</hi> his hands and head having been washed, and he having only dirtied his feet in walking home. Peter had gone from one extreme to the other. At first he would not let Christ wash his feet; and now he overlooks what Christ had done for him in his baptism, and what was signified thereby, and cries out to have his hands and head washed. Now Christ directs him into the meaning; he must have his feet washed, but not his hands and head. [1.] See here what is the comfort and privilege of such as are in a justified state; they are washed by Christ, and are <hi type="italic">clean every whit,</hi> that is, they are graciously accepted of God, as if they were so; and, though they offend, yet they need not, upon their repentance, be again put into a justified state, for then should they often be baptized. The evidence of a justified state may be clouded, and the comfort of it suspended, when yet the charter of it is not vacated or taken away. Though we have occasion to repent daily, God's gifts and callings are without repentance. The heart may be swept and garnished, and yet still remain the devil's palace; but, if it be washed, it belongs to Christ, and he will not lose it. [2.] See what ought to be the daily care of those who through grace are in a justified state, and that is to wash their feet; to cleanse themselves from the guilt they contract daily through infirmity and inadvertence, by the renewed exercise of repentance, with a believing application of the virtue of Christ's blood. We must also wash our feet by constant watchfulness against every thing that is defiling, for we must cleanse our way, and cleanse our feet <hi type="italic">by taking heed thereto,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.9">Ps. cxix. 9</reference>. The priests, when they were consecrated, were washed with water; and, though they did not need afterwards to be so washed all over, yet, whenever they went in to minister, they must wash their feet and hands at the laver, on pain of death, <reference osisRef="Exod.30.19-Exod.30.20">Exod. xxx. 19, 20</reference>. The provision made for our cleansing should not make us presumptuous, but the more cautious. <hi type="italic">I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?</hi> From yesterday's pardon, we should fetch an argument against this day's temptation. <div eID="gen27952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27953" type="x-p"/> (2.) With reflection upon Judas: <hi type="italic">And you are clean, but not all,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.13.10-John.13.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. He pronounces his disciples clean, clean <hi type="italic">through the word he had spoken to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.3">ch. xv. 3</reference>. He washed them himself, and then said, <hi type="italic">You are clean;</hi> but he excepts Judas: <hi type="italic">not all;</hi> they were all baptized, even Judas, yet not all clean; many have the sign that have not the thing signified. Note, [1.] Even among those who are called disciples of Christ, and profess relation to him, there are some who are not clean, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.12">Prov. xxx. 12</reference>. [2.] The Lord knows those that are his, and those that are not, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2 Tim. ii. 19</reference>. The eye of Christ can separate between the precious and the vile, the clean and the unclean. [3.] When those that have called themselves disciples afterwards prove traitors, their apostasy at last is a certain evidence of their hypocrisy all along. [4.] Christ sees it necessary to let his disciples know that they are not all clean; that we may all be jealous over ourselves (<hi type="italic">Is it I? Lord, is it I</hi> that am among the clean, yet not clean?) and that, when hypocrites are discovered, it may be no surprise nor stumbling to us. <div eID="gen27953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27954" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ washed his disciples' feet to set before us an example. This explication he gave of what he had done, when he had done it, <reference osisRef="John.13.12-John.13.17">v. 12-17</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen27954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27955" type="x-p"/> 1. With what solemnity he gave an account of the meaning of what he had done (<reference osisRef="John.13.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">After he had washed their feet,</hi> he said, <hi type="italic">Know you what I have done?</hi> <div eID="gen27955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27956" type="x-p"/> (1.) He adjourned the explication till he had finished the transaction, [1.] To try their submission and implicit obedience. What he did they should not know till afterwards, that they might learn to acquiesce in his will when they could not give a reason for it. [2.] Because it was proper to finish the riddle before he unriddled it. Thus, as to his whole undertaking, when his sufferings were finished, when he had resumed the garments of his exalted state and was ready to sit down again, then he <hi type="italic">opened the understandings of his disciples,</hi> and poured out his Spirit, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.45-Luke.24.46">Luke xxiv. 45, 46</reference>. <div eID="gen27956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27957" type="x-p"/> (2.) Before he explained it, he asked them if they could construe it: <hi type="italic">Know you what I have done to you?</hi> He put this question to them, not only to make them sensible of their ignorance, and the need they had to be instructed (as <reference osisRef="Zech.4.5">Zech. iv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.13">13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Knowest thou not what these be? and I said, No, my Lord</hi>), but to raise their desires and expectations of instruction: "I <hi type="italic">would have you know,</hi> and, if you will give attention, I will tell you." Note, It is the will of Christ that sacramental signs should be explained, and that his people should be acquainted with the meaning of them; otherwise, though ever so significant, to those who know not the thing signified they are insignificant. Hence they are directed to ask, <hi type="italic">What mean you by this service?</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.12.26">Exod. xii. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen27957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27958" type="x-p"/> 2. Upon what he grounds that which he had to say (<reference osisRef="John.13.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You call me Master and Lord,</hi> you give me those titles, in speaking of me, in speaking to me, and <hi type="italic">you say well,</hi> for <hi type="italic">so I am;</hi> you are in the relation of scholars to me, and I do the part of a master to you." Note, (1.) Jesus Christ is our Master and Lord; he that is our Redeemer and Saviour is, in order to that, our Lord and Master. He is our Master, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">didaskalos</hi></hi>—our teacher and instructor in all necessary truths and rules, as a prophet revealing to us the will of God. He is our Lord, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kyrios</hi></hi>—our ruler and owner, that has authority over us and propriety in us. (2.) It becomes the disciples of Christ to call him Master and Lord, not in compliment, but in reality; not by constraint, but with delight. Devout Mr. Herbert, when he mentioned the name of Christ, used to add, my Master; and thus expresses himself concerning it in one of his poems: <div eID="gen27958" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen27959"/> <l level="1" sID="gen27960"/>How sweetly doth my Master sound, my Master!<l eID="gen27960" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen27961"/>As ambergris leaves a rich scent unto the taster,<l eID="gen27961" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen27962"/>So do these words a sweet content, an oriental fragrancy, my Master.<l eID="gen27962" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen27959"/> <div sID="gen27963" type="x-p"/> (3.) Our calling Christ Master and Lord is an obligation upon us to receive and observe the instruction he gives us. Christ would thus pre-engage their obedience to a command that was displeasing to flesh and blood. If Christ be our Master and Lord, be so by our own consent, and we have often called him so, we are bound in honour and honesty to be observant of him. <div eID="gen27963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27964" type="x-p"/> 3. The lesson which he hereby taught: <hi type="italic">You also ought to wash one another's feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.13.14">v. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen27964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27965" type="x-p"/> (1.) Some have understood this literally, and have thought these words amount to the institution of a standing ordinance in the church; that Christians should, in a solemn religious manner, <hi type="italic">wash one another's feet,</hi> in token of their condescending love to one another. St. Ambrose took it so, and practised it in the church of Milan. St. Austin saith that those Christians who did not do it with their hands, yet (he hoped) did it with their hearts in humility; but he saith, It is much better to do it with the hands also, when there is occasion, as <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.10">1 Tim. v. 10</reference>. What Christ has done Christians should not disdain to do. Calvin saith that the pope, in the annual observance of this ceremony on Thursday in the passion week, is rather Christ's ape than his follower, for the duty enjoined, in conformity to Christ, was <hi type="italic">mutual: Wash one another's feet.</hi> And Jansenius saith, It is done, <hi type="italic">Frigid&#232; et dissimiliter—Frigidly, and unlike the primitive model.</hi> <div eID="gen27965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27966" type="x-p"/> (2.) But doubtless it is to be understood figuratively; it is an instructive sign, but not sacramental, as the eucharist. This was a parable to the eye; and three things our Master hereby designed to teach us:—[1.] A humble condescension. We must learn of our Master to be <hi type="italic">lowly in heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Matt. xi. 29</reference>), and walk with all lowliness; we must think meanly of ourselves and respectfully of our brethren, and deem nothing below us but sin; we must say of that which seems mean, but has a tendency to the glory of God and our brethren's good, as David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.22">2 Sam. vi. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">If this be to be vile, I will be yet more vile.</hi> Christ had often taught his disciples humility, and they had forgotten the lesson; but now he teaches them in such a way as surely they could never forget. [2.] A condescension to be serviceable. To wash one another's feet is to stoop to the meanest offices of love, for the real good and benefit one of another, as blessed Paul, who, though free from all, made himself <hi type="italic">servant of all;</hi> and the blessed Jesus, who <hi type="italic">came not to be ministered unto, but to minister.</hi> We must not grudge to take care and pains, and to spend time, and to diminish ourselves for the good of those to whom we are not under any particular obligations, even of our inferiors, and such as are not in a capacity of making us any requital. Washing the feet after travelling contributes both to the decency of the person and to his ease, so that to wash one another's feet is to consult both the credit and the comfort one of another, to do what we can both to advance our brethren's reputation and to make their minds easy. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.24">1 Cor. x. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">Heb. vi. 10</reference>. The duty is <hi type="italic">mutual;</hi> we must both accept help from our brethren and afford help to our brethren. [3.] A serviceableness to the sanctification one of another: <hi type="italic">You ought to wash one another's feet,</hi> from the pollutions of sin. Austin takes it in this sense, and many others. We cannot satisfy for one another's sins, this is peculiar to Christ, but we may help to purify one another from sin. We must in the first place wash ourselves; this charity must begin at home (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.5">Matt. vii. 5</reference>), but it must not end there; we must sorrow for the failings and follies of our brethren, much more for their gross pollutions (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.2">1 Cor. v. 2</reference>), must wash our brethren's polluted feet in tears. We must faithfully reprove them, and do what we can to bring them to repentance (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">Gal. vi. 1</reference>), and we must admonish them, to prevent their falling into the mire; this is washing their feet. <div eID="gen27966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27967" type="x-p"/> 4. Here is the ratifying and enforcing of this command from the example of what Christ had now done: <hi type="italic">If I your Lord and Master have</hi> done it to you, you ought to do it <hi type="italic">to one another.</hi> He shows the cogency of this argument in two things:— <div eID="gen27967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27968" type="x-p"/> (1.) I am <hi type="italic">your Master,</hi> and you are my disciples, and therefore you ought to <hi type="italic">learn of me</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.13.15">v. 15</reference>); for in this, as in other things, <hi type="italic">I have given you an example,</hi> that <hi type="italic">you should do</hi> to others <hi type="italic">as I have done</hi> to you. Observe, [1.] What a good teacher Christ is. He teaches by example as well as doctrine, and for this end came into this world, and dwelt among us, that he might set us a copy of all those graces and duties which his holy religion teaches; and it is a copy without one false stroke. Hereby he made his own laws more intelligible and honourable. Christ is a commander like Gideon, who said to his soldiers, <hi type="italic">Look on me, and do likewise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.7.17">Judg. vii. 17</reference>); like Abimelech, who said, <hi type="italic">What you have seen me do, make haste and do as I have done</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.48">Judg. ix. 48</reference>); and like Cæsar, who called his soldiers, not <hi type="italic">milites—soldiers,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">commilitones—fellow-soldiers,</hi> and whose usual word was, not <hi type="italic">Ite illue,</hi> but <hi type="italic">Venite huc;</hi> not <hi type="italic">Go,</hi> but <hi type="italic">Come.</hi> [2.] What good scholars we must be. We must <hi type="italic">do as he hath done;</hi> for therefore he gave us a copy, that we should write after it, that we might be as he was in this world (<reference osisRef="1John.4.17">1 John iv. 17</reference>), and walk <hi type="italic">as he walked,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.6">1 John ii. 6</reference>. Christ's example here in is to be followed by ministers in particular, in whom the graces of humility and holy love should especially appear, and by the exercise thereof they effectually serve the interests of their Master and the ends of their ministry. When Christ sent his apostles abroad as his agents, it was with this charge, that they should not take state upon them, nor carry things with a high hand, but <hi type="italic">become all things to all men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.22">1 Cor. ix. 22</reference>. What I have done to your dirty feet that do you to the polluted souls of sinners; <hi type="italic">wash them.</hi> Some who suppose this to have been done at the passover supper think it intimates a rule in admitting communicants to the Lord's-supper, to see that they be first washed and cleansed by reformation and a blameless conversation, and then take them in to <hi type="italic">compass God's altar.</hi> But all Christians likewise are here taught to condescend to each other in love, and to do it as Christ did it, unasked, unpaid; we must not be mercenary in the services of love, nor do them with reluctancy. <div eID="gen27968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27969" type="x-p"/> (2.) I am <hi type="italic">your Master,</hi> and you are my disciples, and therefore you cannot think it below you to do that, how mean soever it may seem, which you have seen me do, for (<reference osisRef="John.13.16">v. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">the servant is not greater than his Lord, neither he that is sent,</hi> though sent with all the pomp and power of an ambassador, <hi type="italic">greater than he that sent him.</hi> Christ had urged this (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.24-Matt.10.25">Matt. x. 24, 25</reference>) as a reason why they should not think it strange if they suffered as he did; here he urges it as a reason why they should not think it much to humble themselves as he did. What he did not think a disparagement to him, they must not think a disparagement to them. Perhaps the disciples were inwardly disgusted at this precept of washing one another's feet, as inconsistent with the dignity they expected shortly to be preferred to. To obviate such thoughts, Christ reminds them of their place as his servants; they were not better men than their Master, and what was consistent with his dignity was much more consistent with theirs. If he was humble and condescending, it ill became them to be proud and assuming. Note, [1.] We must take good heed to ourselves, lest Christ's gracious condescensions to us, and advancements of us, through the corruption of nature occasion us to entertain high thoughts of ourselves or low thoughts of him. We need to be put in mind of this, that we are not <hi type="italic">greater than our Lord.</hi> [2.] Whatever our Master was pleased to condescend to in favour to us, we should much more condescend to in conformity to him. Christ, by humbling himself, has dignified humility, and put an honour upon it, and obliged his followers to think nothing below them but sin. We commonly say to those who disdain to do such or such a thing, As good as you have done it, and been never the worse thought of; and true indeed it is, if our Master has done it. When we see our Master serving, we cannot but see how ill it becomes us to be domineering.
entries.8eb22ee432377458f4eda5a8aa142e85febd196d: <div eID="gen27969" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Treachery of Judas Foretold; The Anxiety of the Disciples.</title> <div sID="gen27970" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now I tell you before it come, that, when it is come to pass, ye may believe that I am <hi type="italic">he.</hi> <hi type="super">20</hi> Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that receiveth whomsoever I send receiveth me; and he that receiveth me receiveth him that sent me. <hi type="super">21</hi> When Jesus had thus said, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me. 22 Then the disciples looked one on another, doubting of whom he spake. <hi type="super">23</hi> Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved. <hi type="super">24</hi> Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, that he should ask who it should be of whom he spake. <hi type="super">25</hi> He then lying on Jesus' breast saith unto him, Lord, who is it? <hi type="super">26</hi> Jesus answered, He it is, to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped <hi type="italic">it.</hi> And when he had dipped the sop, he gave <hi type="italic">it</hi> to Judas Iscariot, <hi type="italic">the son</hi> of Simon. <hi type="super">27</hi> And after the sop Satan entered into him. Then said Jesus unto him, That thou doest, do quickly. <hi type="super">28</hi> Now no man at the table knew for what intent he spake this unto him. 29 For some <hi type="italic">of them</hi> thought, because Judas had the bag, that Jesus had said unto him, Buy <hi type="italic">those things</hi> that we have need of against the feast; or, that he should give something to the poor. <hi type="super">30</hi> He then having received the sop went immediately out: and it was night. <div eID="gen27970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27971" type="x-p"/> We have here the discovery of Judas's plot to betray his Master. Christ knew it from the beginning; but now first he discovered it to his disciples, who did not expect Christ should be betrayed, though he had often told them so, much less did they suspect that one of them should do it. Now here, <div eID="gen27971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27972" type="x-p"/> I. Christ gives them a general intimation of it (<reference osisRef="John.13.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">I speak not of you all,</hi> I cannot expect you will all do these things, for <hi type="italic">I know whom I have chosen,</hi> and whom I have passed by; but the scripture will be fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Ps. xli. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.</hi> He does not yet speak out, either of the crime or the criminal, but raises their expectations of a further discovery. <div eID="gen27972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27973" type="x-p"/> 1. He intimates to them that they were not all right. He had said (<reference osisRef="John.13.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">You are clean, but not all.</hi> So here, <hi type="italic">I speak not of you all.</hi> Note, What is said of the excellencies of Christ's disciples cannot be said of all that are called so. The word of Christ is a distinguishing word, which separates <hi type="italic">between cattle and cattle,</hi> and will distinguish thousands into hell who flattered themselves with hopes that they were going to heaven. <hi type="italic">I speak not of you all;</hi> you my disciples and followers. Note, There is a mixture of bad with good in the best societies, a Judas among the apostles; it will be so till we come to the blessed society into which shall enter nothing unclean or disguised. <div eID="gen27973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27974" type="x-p"/> 2. That he himself knew who were right, and who were not: <hi type="italic">I know whom I have chosen,</hi> who the few are that are chosen among the many that are called with the common call. Note, (1.) Those that are chosen, Christ himself had the choosing of them; he nominated the persons he undertook for. (2.) Those that are chosen are known to Christ, for he never forgets any whom he has once had in his thoughts of love, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2 Tim. ii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen27974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27975" type="x-p"/> 3. That in the treachery of him that proved false to him the scripture was fulfilled, which takes off very much both the surprise and offence of the thing. Christ took one into his family whom he foresaw to be a traitor, and did not by effectual grace prevent his being so, <hi type="italic">that the scripture might be fulfilled.</hi> Let it not therefore be a stumbling-block to any; for, though it do not at all lessen Judas's offence, it may lessen our offence at it. The scripture referred to is David's complaint of the treachery of some of his enemies; the Jewish expositors, and ours from them generally understand it of Ahithophel: Grotius thinks it intimates that the death of Judas would be like that of Ahithophel. But because that psalm speaks of David's sickness, of which we read nothing at the time of Ahithophel's deserting him, it may better be understood of some other friend of his, that proved false to him. This our Saviour applies to Judas. (1.) Judas, as an apostle, was admitted to the highest privilege: he did <hi type="italic">eat bread with Christ.</hi> He was familiar with him, and favoured by him, was one of his family, one of those with whom he was intimately conversant. David saith of his treacherous friend, He did eat <hi type="italic">of my bread;</hi> but Christ, being poor, had no bread he could properly call his own. He saith, He did <hi type="italic">eat bread with me;</hi> such as he had by the kindness of his friends, that ministered to him, his disciples had their share of, Judas among the rest. Wherever he went, Judas was welcome with him, did not dine among servants, but sat at table with his Master, ate of the same dish, drank of the same cup, and in all respects fared as he fared. He ate miraculous bread with him, when the loaves were multiplied, ate the passover with him. Note, All that eat bread with Christ are not his disciples indeed. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.3-1Cor.10.5">1 Cor. x. 3-5</reference>. (2.) Judas, as an apostate, was guilty of the basest treachery: he <hi type="italic">lifted up the heel</hi> against Christ. [1.] He forsook him, turned his back upon him, went out from the society of his disciples, <reference osisRef="John.13.30">v. 30</reference>. [2.] He despised him, shook off the dust of his feet against him, in contempt of him and his gospel. Nay, [3.] He became an enemy to him; spurned at him, as wrestlers do at their adversaries, whom they would overthrow. Note, It is no new thing for those that were Christ's seeming friends to prove his real enemies. Those who pretended to magnify him magnify themselves against him, and thereby prove themselves guilty, not only of the basest ingratitude, but the basest treachery and perfidiousness. <div eID="gen27975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27976" type="x-p"/> II. He gives them a reason why he told them beforehand of the treachery of Judas (<reference osisRef="John.13.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Now I tell you before it come,</hi> before Judas has begun to put his wicked plot in execution, <hi type="italic">that when it is come to pass you may,</hi> instead of stumbling at it, be confirmed in your <hi type="italic">belief that I am he,</hi> he that should come." 1. By his clear and certain foresight of things to come, of which in this, as in other instances, he gave incontestable proof, he proved himself to be the true God, before whom all things are naked and open. Christ foretold that Judas would betray him when there was no ground to suspect such a thing, and so proved himself the eternal Word, which is a <hi type="italic">discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.</hi> The prophecies of the New Testament concerning the apostasy of the latter times (which we have, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1-2Thess.2.17">2 Thess. ii.</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.16">1 Tim. iv.</reference>, and in the Apocalypse) being evidently accomplished is a proof that those writings were divinely inspired, and confirms our faith in the whole canon of scripture. 2. By this application of the types and prophecies of the Old Testament to himself, he proved himself to be the true Messiah, to whom <hi type="italic">all the prophets bore witness.</hi> Thus <hi type="italic">it was written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer,</hi> and he suffered just as it was written, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.25-Luke.24.26">Luke xxiv. 25, 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.28">ch. viii. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen27976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27977" type="x-p"/> III. He gives a word of encouragement to his apostles, and all his ministers whom he employs in his service (<reference osisRef="John.13.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that receiveth whomsoever I send receiveth me.</hi> The purport of these words is the same with what we have in other scriptures, but it is not easy to make out their coherence here. Christ had told his disciples that they must humble and abase themselves. "Now," saith he, "though there may be those that will despise you for your condescension, yet there will be those that will do you honour, and shall be honoured for so doing." Those who know themselves dignified by Christ's commission may be content to be vilified in the world's opinion. Or, he intended to silence the scruples of those who, because there was a traitor among the apostles, would be shy of receiving any of them; for, if one of them was false to his Master, to whom would any of them be true? <hi type="italic">Ex uno disce omnes—They are all alike.</hi> No, as Christ will think never the worse of them for Judas's crime, so he will stand by them, and own them, and will raise up such as shall receive them. Those that had received Judas when he was a preacher, and perhaps were converted and edified by his preaching, were never the worse, nor should reflect upon it with any regret, though he afterwards proved a traitor; for he was one whom Christ sent. We cannot know what men are, much less what they will be, but those who appear to be sent of Christ we must receive, till the contrary appear. Though some, by entertaining strangers, have entertained robbers unawares, yet we must still be hospitable, for thereby some have entertained angels. The abuses put upon our charity, though ordered with ever so much discretion, will neither justify our uncharitableness, nor lose us the reward of our charity. 1. We are here encouraged to receive ministers as <hi type="italic">sent of Christ: "He that receiveth whomsoever I send,</hi> though weak and poor, and subject to like passions as others (for as the law, so the gospel, <hi type="italic">makes men priests that have infirmity</hi>), yet if he deliver my message, and be regularly called and appointed to do so, and as an officer give himself to the word and prayer, he that entertains him shall be owned as a friend of mine." Christ was now leaving the world, but he would leave an order of men to be his agents, to deliver his word, and those who receive <hi type="italic">this,</hi> in the light and love of it, receive <hi type="italic">him.</hi> To believe the doctrine of Christ, and obey his law, and accept the salvation offered upon the terms proposed; this is receiving those whom Christ sends, and it is <hi type="italic">receiving Christ Jesus the Lord</hi> himself. 2. We are here encouraged to receive Christ as sent of God: <hi type="italic">He that</hi> thus <hi type="italic">receiveth me,</hi> that receiveth Christ in his ministers, receiveth the Father also, for they come upon his errand likewise, baptizing in the name of the Father, as well as of the Son. Or, in general, <hi type="italic">He that receiveth me</hi> as his prince and Saviour receiveth <hi type="italic">him that sent me</hi> as his portion and felicity. Christ was sent of God, and in embracing his religion we embrace the <hi type="italic">only true</hi> religion. <div eID="gen27977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27978" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ more particularly notifies to them the plot which one of their number was now hatching against him (<reference osisRef="John.13.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">When Jesus had thus said</hi> in general, to prepare them for a more particular discovery, he was <hi type="italic">troubled in spirit,</hi> and showed it by some gesture or sign, and <hi type="italic">he testified,</hi> he solemnly declared it (<hi type="italic">cum animo testandi—with the solemnity of a witness on oath), "One of you shall betray me;</hi> one of you my apostles and constant followers." None indeed could be said to <hi type="italic">betray</hi> him but those in whom he reposed a confidence, and who were the witnesses of his retirements. This did not determine Judas to the sin by any fatal necessity; for, though the event did follow according to the prediction, yet not from the prediction. Christ is not the author of sin; yet as to this heinous sin of Judas, 1. Christ foresaw it; for even that which is secret and future, and hidden from the eyes of all living, naked and open before the eyes of Christ. He <hi type="italic">knows what is in men</hi> better than they do themselves (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.12">2 Kings viii. 12</reference>), and therefore sees what will be done by them. <hi type="italic">I knew that thou wouldest deal very treacherously,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa. xlviii. 8</reference>. 2. He foretold it, not only for the sake of the rest of the disciples, but for the sake of Judas himself, that he might take warning, and recover himself out of the snare of the devil. Traitors proceed not in their plots when they find they are discovered; surely Judas, when he finds that his Master knows his design, will retreat in time; if not, it will aggravate his condemnation. 3. He spoke of it with a manifest concern; he was <hi type="italic">troubled in spirit</hi> when he mentioned it. He had often spoken of his own sufferings and death, without any such trouble of spirit as he here manifested when he spoke of the ingratitude and treachery of Judas. This touched him in a tender part. Note, The falls and miscarriages of the disciples of Christ are a great trouble of spirit to their Master; the sins of Christians are the grief of Christ. "What! <hi type="italic">One of you betray me?</hi> You that have received from me such distinguishing favours; you that I had reason to think would be firm to me, that have professed such a respect for me; what iniquity have you found in me that one of you should betray me?" This went to his heart, as the undutifulness of children grieves those who have <hi type="italic">nourished and brought them up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa. i. 2</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.95.10">Ps. xcv. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Isa. liii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen27978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27979" type="x-p"/> V. The disciples quickly take the alarm. They knew their Master would neither deceive them nor jest with them; and therefore <hi type="italic">looked one upon another,</hi> with a manifest concern, <hi type="italic">doubting of whom he spake.</hi> 1. By looking one upon another they evinced the trouble they were in upon this notice given them; it struck such a horror upon them that they knew not well which way to look, nor what to say. They saw their Master troubled, and therefore they were troubled. This was at a feast where they were cheerfully entertained; but hence we must be taught to rejoice with trembling, and as though we rejoiced not. When David wept for his son's rebellion, all his followers wept with him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2 Sam. xv. 30</reference>); so Christ's disciples here. Note, That which grieves Christ is, and should be, a grief to all that are his, particularly the scandalous miscarriages of those that are called by his name: <hi type="italic">Who is offended, and I burn not?</hi> 2. Hereby they endeavoured to <hi type="italic">discover</hi> the traitor. They looked wistfully in one another's face, to see who blushed, or, by some disorder in the countenance, manifested guilt in the heart, upon this notice; but, while those who were faithful had their consciences so clear that they could <hi type="italic">lift up their faces without spot,</hi> he that was false had his conscience so seared that he was not ashamed, neither could he blush, and so no discovery could be made in this way. Christ thus perplexed his disciples for a time, and put them into confusion, that he might <hi type="italic">humble them, and prove them,</hi> might excite in them a jealousy of themselves, and an indignation at the baseness of Judas. It is good for us sometimes to be put to a gaze, to be put to a pause. <div eID="gen27979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27980" type="x-p"/> VI. The disciples were solicitous to get their Master to explain himself, and to tell them particularly whom he meant; for nothing but this can put them out of their present pain, for each of them thought he had as much reason to suspect himself as any of his brethren; now, <div eID="gen27980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27981" type="x-p"/> 1. Of all the disciples John was most fit to ask, because he was the favourite, and sat next his Master (<reference osisRef="John.13.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was leaning on Jesus's bosom one of the disciples whom Jesus loved.</hi> It appears that this was John, by comparing <reference osisRef="John.21.20">ch. xxi. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.21.24">24</reference>. Observe, (1.) The particular kindness which Jesus had for him; he was known by this periphrasis, that he was <hi type="italic">the disciple whom Jesus loved.</hi> He loved them all (<reference osisRef="John.13.1">v. 1</reference>), but John was particularly dear to him. His name signifies <hi type="italic">gracious.</hi> Daniel, who was honoured with the revelations of the Old Testament, as John of the New, was <hi type="italic">a man greatly beloved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.23">Dan. ix. 23</reference>. Note, Among the disciples of Christ some are dearer to him than others. (2.) His place and posture at this time: He was <hi type="italic">leaning on Jesus's bosom.</hi> Some say that it was the fashion in those countries to sit at meat in a leaning posture, so that the second lay in the bosom of the first, and so on, which does not seem probable to me, for in such a posture as this they could neither eat nor drink conveniently; but, whether this was the case or not, John now <hi type="italic">leaned on Christ's bosom,</hi> and it seems to be an extraordinary expression of endearment used at this time. Note, There are some of Christ's disciples whom he lays in his bosom, who have more free and intimate communion with him than others. The Father loved the Son, and laid him <hi type="italic">in his bosom</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">ch. i. 18</reference>), and believers are in like manner one with Christ, <reference osisRef="John.17.21">ch. xvii. 21</reference>. This honour all the saints shall have shortly in the bosom of Abraham. Those who lay themselves at Christ's feet, he will lay in his bosom. (3.) Yet he conceals his name, because he himself was the penman of the story. He put this instead of his name, to show that he was pleased with it; it is his title of honour, that he was <hi type="italic">the disciple whom Jesus loved,</hi> as in David's and Solomon's court there was one that was the <hi type="italic">king's friend;</hi> yet he does not put his name down, to show that he was not proud of it, nor would seem to boast of it. Paul in a like case saith, <hi type="italic">I knew a man in Christ.</hi> <div eID="gen27981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27982" type="x-p"/> 2. Of all the disciples Peter was most forward to know, <reference osisRef="John.13.24">v. 24</reference>. Peter, sitting at some distance, beckoned to John, by some sign or other, to ask. Peter was generally the leading man, most apt to put himself forth; and, where men's natural tempers lead them to be thus bold in answering and asking, if kept under the laws of humility and wisdom, they make men very serviceable. God gives his gifts variously; but that the forward men in the church may not think too well of themselves, nor the modest be discouraged, it must be noted that it was not Peter, but John, that was the beloved disciple. Peter was desirous to know, not only that he might be sure it was not he, but that, knowing who it was, they might withdraw from him, and guard against him, and, if possible, prevent his design. It were a desirable thing, we should think, to know who in the church will deceive us; yet let this suffice—Christ knows, though we do not.
