The reason why Peter did not himself ask was because John had a much fairer opportunity, by the advantage of his seat at table, to whisper the question into the ear of Christ, and to receive a like private answer. It is good to improve our interest in those that are near to Christ, and to engage their prayers for us. Do we know any that we have reason to think lie in Christ's bosom? Let us beg of them to speak a good word for us. <div eID="gen27982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27983" type="x-p"/> 3. The question was asked accordingly (<reference osisRef="John.13.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">He then, lying at the breast of Jesus,</hi> and so having the convenience of whispering with him, <hi type="italic">saith unto him, Lord, who is it?</hi> Now here John shows, (1.) A regard to his fellow-disciple, and to the motion he made. Though Peter had not the honour he had at this time, yet he did not therefore disdain to take the hint and intimation he gave him. Note, Those who lie in Christ's bosom may often learn from those who lie at his feet something that will be profitable for them, and be reminded of that which they did not of themselves think of. John was willing to gratify Peter herein, having so fair an opportunity for it. As every one hath received the gift, so let him minister the same for a common good, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.6">Rom. xii. 6</reference>. (2.) A reverence of his Master. Though he whispered this in Christ's ear, yet he called him Lord; the familiarity he was admitted to did not at all lessen his respect for his Master. It becomes us to use a reverence in expression, and to observe a decorum even in our secret devotions, which no eye is a witness to, as well as in public assemblies. The more intimate communion gracious souls have with Christ, the more sensible they are of his worthiness and their own unworthiness, as <reference osisRef="Gen.18.27">Gen. xviii. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen27983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27984" type="x-p"/> 4. Christ gave a speedy answer to this question, but whispered it in John's ear; for it appears (<reference osisRef="John.13.29">v. 29</reference>) that the rest were still ignorant of the matter. <hi type="italic">He it is to whom I shall give a sop,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">psomion</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a morsel, a crust, when I have dipped it</hi> in the sauce. And <hi type="italic">when he had dipped the sop,</hi> John strictly observing his motion, <hi type="italic">he gave it to Judas;</hi> and Judas took it readily enough, not suspecting the design of it, but glad of a savoury bit, to make up his mouth with. (1.) Christ notified the traitor by a sign. He could have told John by name who he was (The adversary and enemy is that wicked Judas, he is the traitor, and none but he); but thus he would exercise the observation of John, and intimate what need his ministers have of a spirit of discerning; for the false brethren we are to stand upon our guard against are not made known to us by words, but by signs; they are to be known to us by <hi type="italic">their fruits,</hi> by <hi type="italic">their spirits;</hi> it requires great diligence and care to form a right judgment upon them. (2.) That sign was a sop which Christ gave him, a very proper sign, because it was the fulfilling of the scripture (<reference osisRef="John.13.18">v. 18</reference>) that the traitor should be one that <hi type="italic">ate bread with him,</hi> that was at this time a fellow-commoner with him. It had likewise a significancy in it, and teaches us, [1.] That Christ sometimes gives sops to traitors; worldly riches, honours, and pleasures are sops (if I may so speak), which Providence sometimes gives into the hands of wicked men. Judas perhaps thought himself a favourite because he had the sop, like Benjamin at Joseph's table, a mess by himself; thus the prosperity of fools, like a stupifying sop, helps to <hi type="italic">destroy them.</hi> [2.] That we must not be outrageous against those whom we know to be very malicious against us. Christ carved to Judas as kindly as to any at the table, though he knew he was then plotting his death. <hi type="italic">If thine enemy hunger, feed him;</hi> this is to do as Christ does. <div eID="gen27984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27985" type="x-p"/> VII. Judas himself, instead of being convinced hereby of his wickedness, was the more confirmed in it, and the warning given him was to him a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death;</hi> for it follows, <div eID="gen27985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27986" type="x-p"/> 1. The devil hereupon took possession of him (<reference osisRef="John.13.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">After the sop, Satan entered into him:</hi> not to make him melancholy, nor drive him distracted, which was the effect of his possessing some; not to hurry him into the fire, nor into the water; happy had it been for him if that had been the worst of it, or if with the swine he had been choked in the sea; but Satan entered into him to possess him with a prevailing prejudice against Christ and his doctrine, and a contempt of him, as one whose life was of small value, to excite in him a covetous desire of the wages of unrighteousness and a resolution to stick at nothing for the obtaining of them. But, <div eID="gen27986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27987" type="x-p"/> (1.) Was not Satan in him before? How then is it said that now <hi type="italic">Satan entered into him?</hi> Judas was all along a devil (<reference osisRef="John.6.70">ch. vi. 70</reference>), a son of perdition, but now Satan gained a more full possession of him, had a <hi type="italic">more abundant entrance</hi> into him. His purpose to betray his Master was now ripened into a fixed resolution; now he returned with seven other spirits more wicked than himself, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.26">Luke xi. 26</reference>. Note, [1.] Though the devil is in every wicked man that does his works (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Eph. ii. 2</reference>), yet sometimes he enters more manifestly and more powerfully than at other times, when he puts them upon some enormous wickedness, which humanity and natural conscience startle at. [2.] Betrayers of Christ have much of the devil in them. Christ speaks of the sin of Judas as greater than that of any of his persecutors. <div eID="gen27987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27988" type="x-p"/> (2.) How came Satan to enter into him <hi type="italic">after the sop?</hi> Perhaps he was presently aware that it was the discovery of him, and it made him desperate in his resolutions. Many are made worse by the gifts of Christ's bounty, and are confirmed in their impenitency by that which should have led them to repentance. The <hi type="italic">coals of fire heaped upon their heads,</hi> instead of melting them, harden them. <div eID="gen27988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27989" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ hereupon dismissed him, and delivered him up to his own heart's lusts: <hi type="italic">Then said Jesus unto him, What thou doest, do quickly.</hi> This is not to be understood as either advising him to his wickedness or warranting him in it; but either, (1.) As abandoning him to the conduct and power of Satan. Christ knew that Satan had entered into him, and had peaceable possession; and now he gives him up as hopeless. The various methods Christ had used for his conviction were ineffectual; and therefore, "What thou doest thou wilt do quickly; if thou art resolved to ruin thyself, go on, and take what comes." Note, When the evil spirit is willingly admitted, the good Spirit justly withdraws. Or, (2.) As challenging him to do his worst: "Thou art plotting against me, put thy plot in execution and welcome, the sooner the better, I do not fear thee, I am ready for thee." Note, our Lord Jesus was very forward to suffer and die for us, and was impatient of delay in the perfecting of his undertaking. Christ speaks of Judas's betraying him as a thing he was now doing, though he was only purposing it. Those who are contriving and designing mischief are, in God's account, doing mischief. <div eID="gen27989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27990" type="x-p"/> 3. Those that were at table understood not what he meant, because they did not hear what he whispered to John (<reference osisRef="John.13.28-John.13.29">v. 28, 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">No man at table,</hi> neither the disciples nor any other of the guests, except John, <hi type="italic">knew for what intent</hi> he spoke this to him. (1.) They did not suspect that Christ said it to Judas as a traitor, because it did not enter into their heads that Judas was such a one, or would prove so. Note, It is an excusable dulness in the disciples of Christ not to be quick-sighted in their censures. Most are ready enough to say, when they hear harsh things spoken in general, Now such a one is meant, and now such a one; but Christ's disciples were so well taught to love one another that they could not easily learn to suspect one another; <hi type="italic">charity thinks no evil.</hi> (2.) They therefore took it for granted that he said it to him as a trustee, or treasurer of the household, giving him order for the laying out of some money. Their surmises in this case discover to us for what uses and purposes our Lord Jesus commonly directed payments out of that little stock he had, and so teach us how to honour the Lord with our substance. They concluded something was to be laid out, either, [1.] In works of piety: <hi type="italic">Buy those things that we have need of against the feast.</hi> Though he borrowed a room to eat the passover in, yet he bought in provision for it. That is to be reckoned well bestowed which is laid out upon <hi type="italic">those things we have need of</hi> for the maintenance of God's ordinances among us; and we have the less reason to grudge that expense now because our gospel-worship is far from being so chargeable as the legal worship was. [2.] Or in works of charity: <hi type="italic">That he should give something to the poor.</hi> By this it appears, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That our Lord Jesus, though he lived upon alms himself (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.3">Luke viii. 3</reference>), yet gave alms to the poor, a little out of a little. Though he might very well be excused, not only because he was poor himself, but because he did so much good in other ways, curing so many <hi type="italic">gratis;</hi> yet, to set us an example, he gave, for the relief of the poor, out of that which he had for the subsistence of his family; see <reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Eph. iv. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That the time of a religious feast was thought a proper time for works of charity. When he celebrated the passover he ordered something for the poor. When we experience God's bounty to us, this should make us bountiful to the poor. <div eID="gen27990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27991" type="x-p"/> 4. Judas hereupon sets himself vigorously to pursue his design against him: He <hi type="italic">went away.</hi> Notice is taken, <div eID="gen27991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27992" type="x-p"/> (1.) Of his speedy departure: <hi type="italic">He went out presently,</hi> and quitted the house, [1.] For fear of being more plainly discovered to the company, for, if he were, he expected they would all fall upon him, and be the death of him, or at least of his project. [2.] He went out as one weary of Christ's company and the society of his apostles. Christ needed not to expel him, he expelled himself. Note, Withdrawing from the communion of the faithful is commonly the first overt-act of a backslider, and the beginning of an apostasy. [3.] <hi type="italic">He went out</hi> to prosecute his design, to look for those with whom he was to make his bargain, and to settle the agreement with them. Now that Satan had got into him he hurried him on with precipitation, lest he should see his error and repent of it. <div eID="gen27992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27993" type="x-p"/> (2.) Of the time of his departure: <hi type="italic">It was night.</hi> [1.] Though it was night, an unseasonable time for business, yet, Satan having entered into him, he made no difficulty of the coldness and darkness of the night. This should shame us out of our slothfulness and cowardice in the service of Christ, that the devil's servants are so earnest and venturous in his service. [2.] Because it was night, and this gave him advantage of privacy and concealment. He was not willing to be <hi type="italic">seen</hi> treating with the chief priests, and therefore chose the dark night as the fittest time for such works of darkness. Those whose deeds are evil love darkness rather than light. See <reference osisRef="Job.24.13">Job xxiv. 13</reference>, &c.
entries.6ede05fa9374a80e24aabfb885844135318f5599: <div eID="gen27993" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Departure Predicted.</title> <div sID="gen27994" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> Therefore, when he was gone out, Jesus said, Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified in him. 32 If God be glorified in him, God shall also glorify him in himself, and shall straightway glorify him. <hi type="super">33</hi> Little children, yet a little while I am with you. Ye shall seek me: and as I said unto the Jews, Whither I go, ye cannot come; so now I say to you. <hi type="super">34</hi> A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. 35 By this shall all <hi type="italic">men</hi> know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another. <div eID="gen27994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27995" type="x-p"/> This and what follows, to the end of <reference osisRef="John.13.31-John.14.33">ch. xiv.</reference>, was Christ's table-talk with his disciples. When supper was done, Judas went out; but what did the Master and his disciples do, whom he left sitting at table? They applied themselves to profitable discourse, to teach us as much as we can to make conversation with our friends at table serviceable to religion. Christ begins this discourse. The more forward we are humbly to promote that communication which is good, and to the use of edifying, the more like we are to Jesus Christ. Those especially that by their place, reputation, and gifts, <hi type="italic">command the company,</hi> to whom <hi type="italic">men give ear,</hi> ought to use the interest they have in other respects as an opportunity of doing them good. Now our Lord Jesus discourses with them (and probably discourses much more largely than is here recorded), <div eID="gen27995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27996" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning the great mystery of his own death and sufferings, about which they were as yet so much in the dark that they could not persuade themselves to expect the thing itself, much less did they understand the meaning of it; and therefore Christ gives them such instructions concerning it as made the offence of the cross to cease. Christ did not begin this discourse till Judas was gone out, for he was a false brother. The presence of wicked people is often a hindrance to good discourse. When Judas <hi type="italic">was gone out,</hi> Christ said, <hi type="italic">now is the Son of man glorified;</hi> now that Judas is discovered and discarded, who was a spot in their love-feast and a scandal to their family, <hi type="italic">now is the Son of man glorified.</hi> Note, Christ is glorified by the purifying of Christian societies: corruptions in his church are a reproach to him; the purging out of those corruptions rolls away the reproach. Or, rather, now Judas was gone to set the wheels a-going, in order to his being put to death, and the thing was likely to be effected shortly: <hi type="italic">Now is the Son of man glorified,</hi> meaning, <hi type="italic">Now he is crucified.</hi> <div eID="gen27996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27997" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is something which Christ instructs them in, concerning his sufferings, that was very <hi type="italic">comforting.</hi> <div eID="gen27997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27998" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he should himself be glorified in them. Now the Son of man is to be exposed to the greatest ignominy and disgrace, to be despitefully used to the last degree, and dishonoured both by the cowardice of his friends and the insolence of his enemies; yet <hi type="italic">now he is glorified;</hi> For, [1.] Now he is to obtain a glorious victory over Satan and all the powers of darkness, to spoil them, and triumph over them. He is now <hi type="italic">girding on the harness,</hi> to take the field against these adversaries of God and man, with as great an assurance as if he had <hi type="italic">put it off.</hi> [2.] Now he is to work out a glorious deliverance for his people, by his death to reconcile them to God, and bring in an everlasting righteousness and happiness for them; to shed that blood which is to be an inexhaustible fountain of joys and blessings to all believers. [3.] Now he is to give a glorious example of self-denial and patience under the cross, courage and contempt of the world, zeal for the glory of God, and love to the souls of men, such as will make him to be for ever admired and had in honour. Christ had been glorified in many miracles he had wrought, and yet he speaks of his being glorified <hi type="italic">now</hi> in his sufferings, as if that were more than all his other glories in his humble state. <div eID="gen27998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27999" type="x-p"/> (2.) That God the Father should be glorified in them. The sufferings of Christ were, [1.] The satisfaction of God's justice, and so God was glorified in them. Reparation was thereby made with great advantage for the wrong done him in his honour by the sin of man. The ends of the law were abundantly answered, and the glory of his government effectually asserted and maintained. [2.] They were the manifestation of his holiness and mercy. The attributes of God shine brightly in creation and providence, but much more in the work of redemption; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">1 Cor. i. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>. God is love, and herein he hath commended his love. <div eID="gen27999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28000" type="x-p"/> (3.) That he should himself be greatly glorified after them, in consideration of God's being greatly glorified by them, <reference osisRef="John.13.32">v. 32</reference>. Observe how he enlarges upon it. [1.] He is sure that God will glorify him; and those whom God glorifies are glorious indeed. Hell and earth set themselves to vilify Christ, but God resolved to glorify him, and he did it. He glorified him in his sufferings by the amazing signs and wonders, both in heaven and earth, which attended them, and extorted even from his crucifiers an acknowledgment that he was the Son of God. But especially after his sufferings he glorified him, when he set him <hi type="italic">at his own right hand,</hi> gave him a <hi type="italic">name above every name.</hi> [2.] That he will glorify him <hi type="italic">in himself</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en heauto</hi></hi>. Either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In Christ himself. He will glorify him in his own person, and not only in his kingdom among men. This supposes his speedy resurrection. A common person may be honoured after his death, in his memory or posterity, but Christ was honoured in <hi type="italic">himself.</hi> Or, <hi type="italic">secondly,</hi> in God himself. God will glorify him <hi type="italic">with himself,</hi> as it is explained, <reference osisRef="John.17.5">ch. xvii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">He shall sit down with the Father upon his throne,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev. iii. 21</reference>. This is true glory. [3.] That he will glorify him straightway. He looked upon the joy and glory set before him, not only as great, but as near; and his sorrows and sufferings short and soon over. Good services done to earthly princes often remain long unrewarded; but Christ had his preferments presently. It was but forty hours (or not so much) from his death to his resurrection, and forty days thence to his ascension, so that it might well be said that he was <hi type="italic">straightway glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Ps. xvi. 10</reference>. [4.] All this in consideration of God's being glorified in and by his sufferings: <hi type="italic">Seeing God is glorified in him,</hi> and receives honour from his sufferings, God shall in like manner glorify him in himself, and give honour to him. Note, <hi type="italic">first,</hi> In the exaltation of Christ there was a regard had to his humiliation, and a reward given for it. <hi type="italic">Because he humbled himself, therefore God highly exalted him.</hi> If the Father be so great a gainer in his glory by the death of Christ, we may be sure that the Son shall be no loser in his. See the covenant between them, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those who mind the business of glorifying God no doubt shall have the happiness of being glorified with him. <div eID="gen28000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28001" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is something that Christ instructs them in, concerning his sufferings, which was <hi type="italic">awakening,</hi> for as yet they were slow of heart to understand it (<reference osisRef="John.13.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Little children, yet a little while I am with you,</hi> &c. Two things Christ here suggests, to quicken his disciples to improve their present opportunities; two serious words:— <div eID="gen28001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28002" type="x-p"/> (1.) That his stay in this world, to be with them here, they would find to be very short. <hi type="italic">Little children.</hi> This compellation does not bespeak so much their weakness as his tenderness and compassion; he speaks to them with the affection of a father, now that he is about to leaven them, and to leave blessings with them. Know this, then, that <hi type="italic">yet a little while I am with you.</hi> Whether we understand this as referring to his death or his ascension it comes much to one; he had but a little time to spend with them, and therefore, [1.] Let them improve the advantage they now had. If they had any good question to ask, if they would have any advice, instruction, or comfort, let them speak quickly; for <hi type="italic">yet a little while I am with you.</hi> We must make the best of the helps we have for our souls while we have them, because we shall not have them long; they will be taken from us, or we from them. [2.] Let them not doat upon his bodily presence, as if their happiness and comfort were bound up in that; no, they must think of living without it; not be always little children, but go alone, without their nurses. Ways and means are appointed but for a <hi type="italic">little while,</hi> and are not to be rested in, but pressed through to our rest, to which they have a reference. <div eID="gen28002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28003" type="x-p"/> (2.) That their following him to the other world, to be with him there, they would find to be very difficult. What he had said to the Jews (<reference osisRef="John.7.34">ch. vii. 34</reference>) he saith to his disciples; for they have need to be quickened by the same considerations that are propounded for the convincing and awakening of sinners. Christ tells them here, [1.] That when he was gone they would feel the want of him; <hi type="italic">You shall seek me,</hi> that is "you shall wish you had me again with you." We are often taught the worth of mercies by the want of them. Though the presence of the Comforter yielded them real and effectual relief in straits and difficulties, yet it was not such a <hi type="italic">sensible</hi> satisfaction as his bodily presence would have been to those who had been used to it. But observe, Christ said to the Jews, You shall seek me and <hi type="italic">not find me;</hi> but to the disciples he only saith, <hi type="italic">You shall seek me,</hi> intimating that though they should not find his bodily presence any more than the Jews, yet they should find that which was tantamount, and should not seek in vain. When they sought his body in the sepulchre, though they did not find it, yet they sought to good purpose. [2.] That whither he went they <hi type="italic">could not come,</hi> which suggests to them high thoughts of him, who was going to an invisible inaccessible world, to dwell in that <hi type="italic">light which none can approach unto;</hi> and also low thoughts of themselves, and serious thoughts of their future state. Christ tells them that they could not follow him (as Joshua told the people that they could not serve the Lord) only to quicken them to so much the more diligence and care. They could not follow him to his cross, for they had not courage and resolution; it appeared that they could not when they all forsook him and fled. Nor could they follow him to his crown, for they had not a sufficiency of their own, nor were their work and warfare yet finished. <div eID="gen28003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28004" type="x-p"/> II. He discourses with them concerning the great duty of brotherly love (<reference osisRef="John.13.34-John.13.35">v. 34, 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall love one another.</hi> Judas was now gone out, and had proved himself a false brother; but they must not therefore harbour such jealousies and suspicions one of another as would be the bane of love: though there was one Judas among them, yet they were not all Judases. Now that the enmity of the Jews against Christ and his followers was swelling to the height, and they must expect such treatment as their Master had, it concerned them by brotherly love to strengthen one another's hands. Three arguments for mutual love are here urged:— <div eID="gen28004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28005" type="x-p"/> 1. The command of their Master (<reference osisRef="John.13.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">A new commandment I give unto you.</hi> He not only commends it as amiable and pleasant, not only counsels it as excellent and profitable, but commands it, and makes it one of the fundamental laws of his kingdom; it goes a-breast with the command of believing in Christ, <reference osisRef="1John.3.23">1 John iii. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.22">1 Pet. i. 22</reference>. It is the command of our ruler, who has a right to give law to us; it is the command of our Redeemer, who gives us this law in order to the curing of our spiritual diseases and the preparing of us for our eternal bliss. It is <hi type="italic">a new commandment;</hi> that is, (1.) It is a renewed commandment; it was a commandment <hi type="italic">from the beginning</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.2.7">1 John ii. 7</reference>), as old as the law of nature, it was the second great commandment of the law of Moses; yet, because it is also one of the great commandments of the New Testament, of Christ the new Lawgiver, it is called a new commandment; it is like an old book in a new edition corrected and enlarged. This commandment has been so corrupted by the traditions of the Jewish church that when Christ revived it, and set it in a true light, it might well be called a <hi type="italic">new commandment.</hi> Laws of revenge and retaliation were so much in vogue, and self-love had so much the ascendant, that the law of brotherly love was forgotten as obsolete and out of date; so that as it came from Christ new, it was new to the people. (2.) It is an excellent command, as a <hi type="italic">new song</hi> is an excellent song, that has an uncommon gratefulness in it. (3.) It is an everlasting command; so strangely new as to be always so; as the <hi type="italic">new covenant,</hi> which shall never decay (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.13">Heb. viii. 13</reference>); it shall be new to eternity, when faith and hope are antiquated. (4.) As Christ gives it, it is <hi type="italic">new.</hi> Before it was, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbour;</hi> now it is, You shall love <hi type="italic">one another;</hi> it is pressed in a more winning way when it is thus pressed as mutual duty owing to one another. <div eID="gen28005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28006" type="x-p"/> 2. The example of their Saviour is another argument for brotherly love: <hi type="italic">As I have loved you.</hi> It is this that makes it a <hi type="italic">new commandment</hi>—that this rule and reason of <hi type="italic">love (as I have loved you</hi>) is perfectly new, and such as had been hidden from ages and generations. Understand this, (1.) Of all the instances of Christ's love to his disciples, which they had already experienced during the time he went in and out among them. He spoke kindly to them, concerned himself heartily for them, and for their welfare, instructed, counselled, and comforted them, prayed with them and for them, vindicated them when they were accused, took their part when they were run down, and publicly owned them to be dearer to him that his <hi type="italic">mother, or sister, or brother.</hi> He reproved them for what was amiss, and yet compassionately bore with their failings, excused them, made the best of them, and passed by many an oversight. Thus he <hi type="italic">had</hi> loved them, and just now washed their feet; and thus they <hi type="italic">must</hi> love one another, and love <hi type="italic">to the end.</hi> Or, (2.) It may be understood of the special instance of love to all his disciples which he was now about to give, in laying down his life for them. <hi type="italic">Greater love hath no man than this,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.13">ch. xv. 13</reference>. Has he thus loved us all? Justly may he expect that we should be loving to one another. Not that we are capable of doing any thing of the <hi type="italic">same nature</hi> for each other (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.7">Ps. xlix. 7</reference>), but we must love one another in some respects after the <hi type="italic">same manner;</hi> we must set this before us as our copy, and take directions from it. Our love to one another must be free and ready, laborious and expensive, constant and persevering; it must be love <hi type="italic">to the souls</hi> one of another. We must also love one another from <hi type="italic">this motive,</hi> and upon this consideration—because Christ has loved us. See <reference osisRef="Rom.15.1 Rom.15.3 Eph.5.2 Eph.5.25 Phil.2.1-Phil.2.5">Rom. xv. 1, 3; Eph. v. 2, 25; Phil. ii. 1-5</reference>. <div eID="gen28006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28007" type="x-p"/> 3. The reputation of their profession (<reference osisRef="John.13.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one to another.</hi> Observe, We must have love, not only show love, but have it in the root and habit of it, and have it when there is not any present occasion to show it; have it <hi type="italic">ready.</hi> "Hereby it will appear that you are indeed my followers by following me in this." Note, Brotherly love is the badge of Christ's disciples. By this he knows them, by this they may know themselves (<reference osisRef="1John.2.14">1 John ii. 14</reference>), and by this others may know them. This is the livery of his family, the distinguishing character of his disciples; this he would have them <hi type="italic">noted for,</hi> as that wherein they excelled all others—their loving one another. This was what their Master was famous for; all that ever heard of him have heard of his love, his great love; and therefore, if you see any people more affectionate one to another than what is common, say, "Certainly these are the followers of Christ, they have been with Jesus." Now by this it appears, (1.) That the heart of Christ was very much upon it, that his disciples <hi type="italic">should love one another.</hi> In this they must be <hi type="italic">singular;</hi> whereas the way of the world is to be <hi type="italic">every one for himself,</hi> they should be hearty for one another. He does not say, <hi type="italic">By this shall men know</hi> that you are my disciples—if you <hi type="italic">work miracles,</hi> for a worker of miracles is but a cypher without charity (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.2">1 Cor. xiii. 1, 2</reference>); but <hi type="italic">if you love one another</hi> from a principle of self-denial and gratitude to Christ. This Christ would have to be the <hi type="italic">proprium</hi> of his religion, the principal note of the true church. (2.) That it is the true honour of Christ's disciples to excel in brotherly love. Nothing will be more effectual than this to recommend them to the esteem and respect of others. See what a powerful attractive it was, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.46-Acts.2.47">Acts ii. 46, 47</reference>. Tertullian speaks of it as the glory of the primitive church that the Christians were known by their affection to one another. Their adversaries took notice of it, and said, <hi type="italic">See how these Christians love one another,</hi> Apol. cap. 39. (3.) That, if the followers of Christ do not love one another, they not only cast an unjust reproach upon their profession, but give just cause to suspect their own sincerity. <hi type="italic">O Jesus! are these thy Christians,</hi> these passionate, malicious, spiteful, ill-natured people? <hi type="italic">Is this thy son's coat?</hi> When our brethren stand in need of help from us, and we have an opportunity of being service able to them, when they differ in opinion and practice from us, or are any ways rivals with or provoking to us, and so we have an occasion to condescend and forgive, in such cases as this it will be known whether we have this badge of Christ's disciples.
entries.7a962718c51c593af1ca2bdfe28448a55d3b3b08: <div eID="gen28007" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Peter's Self-Confidence.</title> <div sID="gen28008" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> Simon Peter said unto him, Lord, whither goest thou? Jesus answered him, Whither I go, thou canst not follow me now; but thou shalt follow me afterwards. <hi type="super">37</hi> Peter said unto him, Lord, why cannot I follow thee now? I will lay down my life for thy sake. <hi type="super">38</hi> Jesus answered him, Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice. <div eID="gen28008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28009" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen28009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28010" type="x-p"/> I. Peter's curiosity, and the check given to that. <div eID="gen28010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28011" type="x-p"/> 1. Peter's question was bold and blunt (<reference osisRef="John.13.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lord, whither goest thou?</hi> referring to what Christ had said (<reference osisRef="John.13.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">Whither I go, you cannot come.</hi> The practical instructions Christ had given them concerning brotherly love he overlooks, and asks no questions upon them, but fastens upon that concerning which Christ purposely kept them in the dark. Note, It is a common fault among us to be more inquisitive concerning things secret, which belong to God only, than concerning things <hi type="italic">revealed, which belong to us and our children,</hi> more desirous to have our curiosity gratified than our consciences directed, to know what is done in heaven than what we may do to get thither. It is easy to observe it in the converse of Christians, how soon a discourse of that which is plain and edifying is dropped, and no more said to it, the subject is exhausted; which in a matter of doubtful disputation runs into an endless strife of words. <div eID="gen28011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28012" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ's answer was instructive. He did not gratify him with any particular account of the world he was going to, nor ever foretold his glories and joys so distinctly as he did his sufferings, but said what he had said before (<reference osisRef="John.13.36">v. 36</reference>): Let this suffice, <hi type="italic">thou canst not follow me now, but shalt follow me hereafter,</hi> (1.) We may understand it of his following him to the cross: "Thou hast not yet strength enough of faith and resolution to drink of my cup;" and it appeared so by his cowardice when Christ was suffering. For this reason, when Christ was seized, he provided for the safety of his disciples. <hi type="italic">Let these go their way,</hi> because they could not <hi type="italic">follow him now.</hi> Christ considers the frame of his disciples, and will not cut out for them that work and hardship which they are not as yet fit for; the day shall be as the strength is. Peter, though designed for martyrdom, cannot follow Christ now, not being come to his full growth, but he <hi type="italic">shall follow</hi> him <hi type="italic">hereafter;</hi> he shall be crucified at last, like his Master. Let him not think that because he escapes suffering now he shall never suffer. From our missing the cross once, we must not infer that we shall never meet it; we may be reserved for greater trials than we have yet known. (2.) We may understand it of his following him to the crown. Christ was now going to his glory, and Peter was very desirous to go with him: "No," saith Christ, "<hi type="italic">thou canst not follow me now,</hi> thou art not yet ripe for heaven, nor hast thou finished thy work on earth. The forerunner must <hi type="italic">first enter to prepare a place</hi> for thee, but <hi type="italic">thou shalt follow me afterwards,</hi> after thou hast fought the good fight, and at the time appointed." Note, Believers must not expect to be glorified as soon as they are effectually called, for there is a wilderness between the Red Sea and Canaan. <div eID="gen28012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28013" type="x-p"/> II. Peter's confidence, and the check given to that. <div eID="gen28013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28014" type="x-p"/> 1. Peter makes a daring protestation of his constancy. He is not content to be left behind, but asks, "<hi type="italic">Lord why cannot I follow thee now?</hi> Dost thou question my sincerity and resolution? I promise thee, if there be occasion, <hi type="italic">I will lay down my life for thy sake.</hi>" Some think Peter had a conceit, as the Jews had in a like case (<reference osisRef="John.7.35">ch. vii. 35</reference>), that Christ was designing a journey or voyage into some remote country, and that he declared his resolution to go along with him wherever he went; but, having heard his Master so often speak of his own sufferings, surely he could not understand him any otherwise than of his going away by death; and he resolves as Thomas did that he will <hi type="italic">go and die with him;</hi> and better die with him than live without him. See here, (1.) What an affectionate love Peter had to our Lord Jesus: "<hi type="italic">I will lay down my life for thy sake,</hi> and I can do no more." I believe Peter spoke as he thought, and though he was inconsiderate he was not insincere, in his resolution. Note, Christ should be dearer to us than our own lives, which therefore, when we are called to it, we should be willing to lay down for his sake, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Acts xx. 24</reference>. (2.) How ill he took it to have it questioned, intimated in that expostulation, "<hi type="italic">Lord, why cannot I follow thee now?</hi> Dost thou suspect my fidelity to thee?" <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.8">1 Sam. xxix. 8</reference>. Note, It is with regret that true love hears its own sincerity arraigned, as <reference osisRef="John.21.17">ch. xxi. 17</reference>. Christ had indeed said that one of them was a devil, but he was discovered, and gone out, and therefore Peter thinks he may speak with the more assurance of his own sincerity; "Lord, I am resolved I will never leave thee, and therefore <hi type="italic">why cannot I follow thee?</hi>" We are apt to think that we can do any thing, and take it amiss to be told that this and the other we cannot do, whereas without Christ we can do nothing. <div eID="gen28014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28015" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ gives him a surprising prediction of his inconstancy, <reference osisRef="John.13.38">v. 38</reference>. Jesus Christ knows us better than we know ourselves, and has many ways of discovering those to themselves whom he loves, and will hide pride from. (1.) He upbraids Peter with his confidence: <hi type="italic">Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake?</hi> Me thinks, he seems to have said this with a smile: "Peter, thy promises are too large, too lavish to be relied on; thou dost not consider with what reluctancy and struggle a life is laid down, and what a hard task it is to die; not so soon done as said." Christ hereby puts Peter upon second thoughts, not that he might retract his resolution, or recede from it, but that he might insert into it that necessary proviso, "Lord, <hi type="italic">thy grace enabling me,</hi> I will lay down my life for thy sake." "Wilt thou undertake to die for me? What! thou that trembledst to walk upon the water to me? What! thou that, when sufferings were spoken of, criedst out, <hi type="italic">Be it far from thee, Lord?</hi> It was an easy thing to leave thy boats and nets to follow me, but not so easy to lay down thy life." His Master himself struggled when it came to his, and <hi type="italic">the disciple is not greater than his Lord.</hi> Note, It is good for us to shame ourselves out of our presumptuous confidence in ourselves. Shall a bruised reed set up for a pillar, or a sickly child undertake to be a champion? What a fool am I to talk so big. (2.) He plainly foretels his cowardice in the critical hour. To stop the mouth of his boasting, lest Peter should say it again, Yea Master, that I will, Christ solemnly asserts it with, <hi type="italic">Verily, verily, I say unto thee, the cock shall not crow till thou hast denied me thrice.</hi> He does not say as afterwards, <hi type="italic">This night,</hi> for it seems to have been two nights before the passover; but, "Shortly thou wilt have denied me thrice within the space of one night; nay, within so short a space as between the first and last crowing of the cock: <hi type="italic">The cock shall not crow,</hi> shall not have crowed his crowing out, till thou has again and again denied me, and that for fear of suffering." The crowing of the cock is mentioned, [1.] To intimate that the trial in which he would miscarry thus should be in the night, which was an improbable circumstance, but Christ's foretelling it was an instance of his infallible foresight. [2.] Because the crowing of the cock was to be the occasion of his repentance, which of itself would not have been if Christ had not put this into the prediction. Christ not only foresaw that Judas would betray him though he only in heart designed it, but he foresaw that Peter would deny him though he did not design it, but the contrary. He knows not only the wickedness of sinners, but the weakness of saints. Christ told Peter, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he would deny him, would renounce and abjure him: "Thou wilt not only not follow me still, but wilt be ashamed to own that ever thou didst follow me." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he would do this not once only by a hasty slip of the tongue, but after he had paused would repeat it a second and third time; and it proved too true. We commonly give it as a reason why the prophecies of scripture are expressed darkly and figuratively, because, if they did <hi type="italic">plainly</hi> describe the event, the accomplishment would thereby either be defeated or necessitated by a fatality inconsistent with human liberty; and yet this plain and express prophecy of Peter's denying Christ did neither, nor did in the least make Christ accessary to Peter's sin. But we may well imagine what a mortification it was to Peter's confidence of his own courage to be told this, and to be told it in such a manner that he durst not contradict it, else he would have said as Hazael, <hi type="italic">What! is thy servant a dog?</hi> This could not but fill him with confusion. Note, The most secure are commonly the least safe; and those most shamefully betray their own weakness that most confidently presume upon their own strength, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.12">1 Cor. x. 12</reference>.  <chapter eID="John.13"/> <div eID="gen28015" type="x-p"/>

entries.c94382292b18824f7a6f56537e227924abb2e718: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15284"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.13.1-John.13.20">Joh 13:1-20</reference>. At the Last Supper Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet--The Discourse Arising Thereupon.</title> <div sID="gen29391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15284"/><hi type="bold">1. when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father--</hi>On these beautiful euphemisms, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.9.31">Lu 9:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.51">Lu 9:51</reference>.<div eID="gen29391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end--</hi>The meaning is, that on the very edge of His last sufferings, when it might have been supposed that He would be absorbed in His own awful prospects, He was so far from forgetting "His own," who were to be left struggling "in the world" after He had "departed out of it to the Father" (<reference osisRef="John.17.11">Joh 17:11</reference>), that in His care for them He seemed scarce to think of Himself save in connection with them: "Herein is love," not only "enduring to the end," but most affectingly manifested when, judging by a human standard, least to be expected. <div eID="gen29392" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2214dc1b11369d502566619f9f3533c4e81896e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15285"/><div sID="gen29393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15285"/><hi type="bold">2. supper being ended--</hi>rather, "being prepared," "being served," or, "going on"; for that it was not "ended" is plain from <reference osisRef="John.13.26">Joh 13:26</reference>.<div eID="gen29393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the devil having now--</hi>or, "already."<div eID="gen29394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put into the heart of Judas ... to betray him--</hi>referring to the agreement he had already made with the chief priests (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.3-Luke.22.6">Lu 22:3-6</reference>). <div eID="gen29395" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7a5a55bd968e7cec0638b4a29ce5e9a699a5943: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15286"/><div sID="gen29396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15286"/><hi type="bold">3. Jesus knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, &c.--</hi>This verse is very sublime, and as a preface to what follows, were we not familiar with it, would fill us with inexpressible surprise. An unclouded perception of His relation to the Father, the commission He held from Him, and His approaching return to Him, possessed His soul. <div eID="gen29396" type="x-p"/>
entries.93627f5ce7473eb86cabac7b53ce9f987623b3cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15287"/><div sID="gen29397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15287"/><hi type="bold">4-5. He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments--</hi>outer garments which would have impeded the operation of washing.<div eID="gen29397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and took a towel and girded himself--</hi>assuming a servant's dress. <div eID="gen29398" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ef274badee74a1c15a6151258bb877699bfb8ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15289"/><div sID="gen29400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15289"/><hi type="bold">6-11. Peter saith ... Lord, dost thou wash my feet?--</hi>Our language cannot bring out the intensely vivid contrast between the "Thou" and the "my," which, by bringing them together, the original expresses, for it is not good English to say, "Lord, Thou my feet dost wash?" But every word of this question is emphatic. Thus far, and in the question itself, there was nothing but the most profound and beautiful astonishment at a condescension to him quite incomprehensible. Accordingly, though there can be no doubt that already Peter's heart rebelled against it as a thing not to be tolerated, Jesus ministers no rebuke as yet, but only bids him wait a little, and he should understand it all. <div eID="gen29400" type="x-p"/>
entries.28bfe505d3ae545e948b3ec9f4041e2792962365: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15294"/><div sID="gen29412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15294"/><hi type="bold">12-15. Know ye what I have done?--</hi>that is, its intent. The question, however, was put merely to summon their attention to His own answer. <div eID="gen29412" type="x-p"/>
entries.7233462da0ea72ea7e297bc50f0e7b3ffc599993: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15297"/><div sID="gen29420" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15297"/><hi type="bold">16-17. The servant is not greater than his lord, &c.--</hi>an oft-repeated saying (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.24">Mt 10:24</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen29420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29421" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them--</hi>a hint that even among real Christians the doing of such things would come lamentably short of the knowing. <div eID="gen29421" type="x-p"/>
entries.883a905bc9bd696ab4013341b4fa992dc817f364: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15298"/><div sID="gen29422" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15298"/><hi type="bold">18-19. I speak not of you all--</hi>the "happy are ye," of <reference osisRef="John.13.17">Joh 13:17</reference>, being on no supposition applicable to Judas.<div eID="gen29422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I know whom I have chosen--</hi>in the higher sense.<div eID="gen29423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But that the scripture may be fulfilled--</hi>that is, one has been added to your number, by no accident or mistake, who is none of Mine, but just that he might fulfil his predicted destiny.<div eID="gen29424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He that eateth bread with me--</hi>"did eat of my bread" (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Psa 41:9</reference>), as one of My family; admitted to the nearest familiarity of discipleship and of social life.<div eID="gen29425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath lifted up his heel against me--</hi>turned upon Me, adding insult to injury. (Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">He 10:29</reference>). In the Psalm the immediate reference is to Ahithophel's treachery against David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.17.1-2Sam.17.23">2Sa 17:1-23</reference>), one of those scenes in which the parallel of his story with that of His great Antitype is exceedingly striking. "The eating bread derives a fearful meaning from the participation in the sacramental supper, a meaning which must be applied for ever to all unworthy communicants, as well as to all betrayers of Christ who eat the bread of His Church" (Stier, with whom, and others, we agree in thinking that Judas partook of the Lord's Supper). <div eID="gen29426" type="x-p"/>
entries.f528a509f56e4cb2826b5852030153a2ac247802: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15300"/><div sID="gen29428" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15300"/><hi type="bold">20. He that receiveth whomsoever I send, receiveth me, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.40">Mt 10:40</reference>). The connection here seems to be that despite the dishonor done to Him by Judas, and similar treatment awaiting themselves, they were to be cheered by the assurance that their office, even as His own, was divine. <div eID="gen29428" type="x-p"/>
entries.223c563b65ad05de39991f5daa0360d5741c6de8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15301"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.13.21-John.13.30">Joh 13:21-30</reference>. The Traitor Indicated--He Leaves the Supper Room.</title> <div sID="gen29429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15301"/><hi type="bold">21. When Jesus had thus said, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, One of you shall betray me--</hi>The announcement of <reference osisRef="John.13.18">Joh 13:18</reference> seems not to have been plain enough to be quite apprehended, save by the traitor himself. He will therefore speak it out in terms not to be misunderstood. But how much it cost Him to do this, appears from the "trouble" that came over His "spirit"--visible emotion, no doubt--before He got it uttered. What wounded susceptibility does this disclose, and what exquisite delicacy in His social intercourse with the Twelve, to whom He cannot, without an effort, break the subject! <div eID="gen29429" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e8702a7f1493d9b94fe7d52d761f2b692b49b31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15302"/><div sID="gen29430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15302"/><hi type="bold">22. the disciples looked one on another, doubting of whom he spake--</hi>Further intensely interesting particulars are given in the other Gospels: (1) "They were exceeding sorrowful" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.22">Mt 26:22</reference>). (2) "They began to inquire among themselves which of them it was that should do this thing" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.23">Lu 22:23</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.3">3</reference>) "They began to say unto Him one by one, Is it I, and another, Is it I?" (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.19">Mr 14:19</reference>). Generous, simple hearts! They abhorred the thought, but, instead of putting it on others, each was only anxious to purge himself and know if he could be the wretch. Their putting it at once to Jesus Himself, as knowing doubtless who was to do it, was the best, as it certainly was the most spontaneous and artless evidence of their innocence. (4) Jesus, apparently while this questioning was going on, added, "The Son of man goeth as it is written of Him, but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! It had been good for that man if he had not been born" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.24">Mt 26:24</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.5">5</reference>) "Judas," last of all, "answered and said, Lord, is it I?" evidently feeling that when all were saying this, if he held his peace, that of itself would draw suspicion upon him. To prevent this the question is wrung out of him, but perhaps, amidst the stir and excitement at the table, in a half-suppressed tone as we are inclined to think the answer also was--"Thou hast said" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.25">Mt 26:25</reference>), or possibly by little more than a sign; for from <reference osisRef="John.13.28">Joh 13:28</reference> it is evident that till the moment when he went out, he was not openly discovered. <div eID="gen29430" type="x-p"/>
entries.04271a82415972da9d107ba76ce01d5d4f8038e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15303"/><div sID="gen29431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15303"/><hi type="bold">23-26. there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved--</hi>Thus modestly does our Evangelist denote himself, as reclining next to Jesus at the table.<div eID="gen29431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Peter ... beckoned to him to ask who it should be of whom he spake--</hi>reclining probably at the corresponding place on the other side of Jesus. <div eID="gen29432" type="x-p"/>
entries.66566566fe53bd380cc1a47d07d34e9c451df4d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15306"/><div sID="gen29438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15306"/><hi type="bold">27-30. after the sop Satan entered into him--</hi>Very solemn are these brief hints of the successive steps by which Judas reached the climax of his guilt. "The devil had already put it into his heart to betray his Lord." Yet who can tell what struggles he went through ere he brought himself to carry that suggestion into effect? Even after this, however, his compunctions were not at an end. With the thirty pieces of silver already in his possession, he seems still to have quailed--and can we wonder? When Jesus stooped to wash his feet, it may be the last struggle was reaching its crisis. But that word of the Psalm, about "one that ate of his bread who would lift up his heel against Him" (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Psa 41:9</reference>) probably all but turned the dread scale, and the still more explicit announcement, that one of those sitting with Him at the table should betray Him, would beget the thought, "I am detected; it is now too late to draw back." At that moment the sop is given; offer of friendship is once more made--and how affectingly! But already "Satan has entered into him," and though the Saviour's act might seem enough to recall him even yet, hell is now in his bosom, and he says within himself, "The die is cast; now let me go through with it"; fear, begone!" (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.43">Mt 12:43</reference>).<div eID="gen29438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Then said Jesus unto him, That thou doest, do quickly--</hi>that is, Why linger here? Thy presence is a restraint, and thy work stands still; thou hast the wages of iniquity, go work for it! <div eID="gen29439" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd3914e66584082b3412933a5cac35653a004e55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15309"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.13.31-John.13.38">Joh 13:31-38</reference>. Discourse after the Traitor's Departure--Peter's Self-Confidence--His Fall Predicted.</title> <div sID="gen29443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15309"/><hi type="bold">31. when he was gone out, Jesus said, Now is the Son of man glorified--</hi>These remarkable words plainly imply that up to this moment our Lord had spoken under a painful restraint, the presence of a traitor within the little circle of His holiest fellowship on earth preventing the free and full outpouring of His heart; as is evident, indeed, from those oft-recurring clauses, "Ye are not all clean," "I <hi type="bold">speak not of you all," &c. "Now" the restraint is removed, and the embankment which kept in the mighty volume of living waters having broken down, they burst forth in a torrent which only ceases on His leaving the supper room and entering on the next stage of His great work--</hi>the scene in the Garden. But with what words is the silence first broken on the departure of Judas? By no reflections on the traitor, and, what is still more wonderful, by no reference to the dread character of His own approaching sufferings. He does not even name them, save by announcing, as with a burst of triumph, that the hour of His glory has arrived! And what is very remarkable, in five brief clauses He repeats this word "glorify" five times, as if to His view a coruscation of glories played at that moment about the Cross. (See on <reference osisRef="John.12.23">Joh 12:23</reference>).<div eID="gen29443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God is glorified in him--</hi>the glory of Each reaching its zenith in the Death of the Cross! <div eID="gen29444" type="x-p"/>
entries.3000770fd067d4be78555f2d71441d0a4dd4f670: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15310"/><div sID="gen29445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15310"/><hi type="bold">32. If God be glorified in him, God shall also--</hi>in return and reward of this highest of all services ever rendered to Him, or capable of being rendered.<div eID="gen29445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glorify him in himself, and ... straightway glorify him--</hi>referring now to the Resurrection and Exaltation of Christ after this service was over, including all the honor and glory then put upon Him, and that will for ever encircle Him as Head of the new creation. <div eID="gen29446" type="x-p"/>
entries.8086d519700bae92b2fd3454a1eac99d168e9bb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15311"/><div sID="gen29447" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15311"/><hi type="bold">33-35. Little children--</hi>From the height of His own glory He now descends, with sweet pity, to His "little children," all now His own. This term of endearment, nowhere else used in the Gospels, and once only employed by Paul (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Ga 4:19</reference>), is appropriated by the beloved disciple himself, who no fewer than seven times employs it in his first Epistle.<div eID="gen29447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ye shall seek me--</hi>feel the want of Me.<div eID="gen29448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29449" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as I said to the Jews--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.7.34">Joh 7:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.21">8:21</reference>). But oh in what a different sense! <div eID="gen29449" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb6f8d81e82a04a94a0f982a9fd720a079f93a38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15314"/><div sID="gen29453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15314"/><hi type="bold">36-38. Peter said--</hi>seeing plainly in these directions how to behave themselves, that He was indeed going from them.<div eID="gen29453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord, whither guest thou?--</hi>having hardly a glimmer of the real truth.<div eID="gen29454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus answered, ... thou canst not follow me now, but thou shalt follow me afterwards--</hi>How different from what He said to the Jews: "Whither I go ye cannot come" (<reference osisRef="John.8.21">Joh 8:21</reference>). <div eID="gen29455" type="x-p"/>

entries.d2dbbe78ed650ef6093fc6425afc9c19ed37e76c: <div eID="gen42512" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen42513" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen42514" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen42514" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen42513" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen42515" type="x-p"/> Christ washes the feet of his disciples, and gives them instructions concerning humility and charity, vv. 1-17. He tells them that one of themselves will betray him, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.18-Joh.13.20">Joh 13:18-20</reference>. The disciples doubting of whom he spoke, Peter desires John to ask him, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.21-Joh.13.25">Joh 13:21-25</reference>. Jesus shows that it is Judas Iscariot, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.26">Joh 13:26</reference>. Satan enters into Judas, and he rises up and leaves the company, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.27-Joh.13.30">Joh 13:27-30</reference>. Christ shows his approaching death, and commands his disciples to love one another, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.31-Joh.13.35">Joh 13:31-35</reference>. Peter, professing strong attachment to Christ, is informed of his denial, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.36-Joh.13.38">Joh 13:36-38</reference>. <div eID="gen42515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42516" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen42516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42517" type="x-p"/> Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew, etc. - Or, as some translate, Now Jesus having known, before the feast of the passover, that his hour was come, etc. The supper mentioned in <reference osisRef="Joh.13.2">Joh 13:2</reference> is supposed to have been that on the Thursday evening, when the feast of the passover began; and though, in our common translation, this passage seems to place the supper before that feast, yet, according to the amended translation, what is here said is consistent with what we read in the other evangelists. See <reference osisRef="Mat.26.2">Mat 26:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.12.1">Joh 12:1</reference>. <div eID="gen42517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42518" type="x-p"/> Having loved his own - His disciples. <div eID="gen42518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42519" type="x-p"/> Which were in the world - Who were to continue longer in its troubles and difficulties. <div eID="gen42519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42520" type="x-p"/> He loved them unto the end - Continued his fervent affection towards them to his latest breath, and gave them that convincing proof of it which is mentioned <reference osisRef="Joh.13.5">Joh 13:5</reference>. That the disciples alone are meant here every man must see.
entries.b8bfbb3d66dd1b395811c5b9ffda97d29f9e08dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen42520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42521" type="x-p"/> And supper being ended - Rather, δειπνου γενομενου, while supper was preparing. To support this new translation of the words, it may be remarked that, from <reference osisRef="Joh.13.26">Joh 13:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.30">Joh 13:30</reference>, it appears that the supper was not then ended: nay, it is probable that it was not then begun; because the washing of feet (<reference osisRef="Joh.13.5">Joh 13:5</reference>) was usually practised by the Jews before they entered upon their meals, as may be gathered from <reference osisRef="Luk.7.44">Luk 7:44</reference>, and from the reason of the custom. I think that John wrote, not γενομενου, but γινομενου, as in BL. Cant. and Origen, which latter reading is approved by several eminent critics, and should be translated as above. By the supper I suppose to be meant, not only the eating of it, but the preparing and dressing of it, and doing all things necessary previously to the eating of it. The devil had, before this time of the supper, put it into Judas's heart to betray his Master. See <reference osisRef="Mat.26.14">Mat 26:14</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Mar.14.10">Mar 14:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.11">Mar 14:11</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Luk.22.3">Luk 22:3</reference>, etc. See also Bishop Pearce, from whose judicious commentary the preceding notes are principally taken. <div eID="gen42521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42522" type="x-p"/> Calmet observes that John, designing only to supply what was omitted by the other evangelists, passes over all the transactions of the Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday, before the passion, and at once goes from Monday evening to Thursday evening. It is remarkable that St. John says nothing about the institution of the holy sacrament, which Matthew, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.26">Mat 26:26</reference>, etc., Mark, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.22">Mar 14:22</reference>, etc., and Luke, <reference osisRef="Luk.22.19">Luk 22:19</reference>, etc., describe so particularly. No other reason can be assigned for this than that he found it completely done by the others, and that he only designed to supply their defects. <div eID="gen42522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42523" type="x-p"/> The devil having now put it into the heart - Judas formed his plot six days before this, on occasion of what happened at the house of Simon the leper: see <reference osisRef="Mat.26.14">Mat 26:14</reference>. Calmet.
entries.5f6c1f762fafdc7c9a4a5281e3cabb4f8551e3c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen42523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42524" type="x-p"/> Knowing that the Father had given, etc. - Our Lord, seeing himself almost at the end of his race, and being about to leave his apostles, thought it necessary to leave them a lesson of humility exemplified by himself, to deliver them from the bad influence of those false ideas which they formed concerning the nature of his kingdom. On all occasions previously to this, the disciples had shown too much attachment to worldly honors and dignities: if this ambition had not been removed, the consequences of it would have been dreadful in the establishment of the religion of Christ; as after his death, it would have divided and infallibly dispersed them. It was necessary therefore to restrain this dangerous passion, and to confirm by a remarkable example what he had so often told them, - that true greatness consisted in the depth of humility, and that those who were the willing servants of all should be the highest in the account of God.
entries.aab2023e3cde681eb39324366c987db1af857c08: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen42524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42525" type="x-p"/> He riseth from supper - Not from eating, as Bishop Pearce has well observed, but from his place at table; probably the dishes were not as yet laid down, though the guests were seated. According to the custom of the Jews and other Asiatics, this washing must have taken place before the supper. See on <reference osisRef="Joh.13.2">Joh 13:2</reference> (note). <div eID="gen42525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42526" type="x-p"/> Laid aside his garments - That is, his gown or upper coat, with the girdle wherewith it was girded close to his tunic or under coat; and, instead of this girdle, he tied a towel about him: <div eID="gen42526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42527" type="x-p"/> 1. that he might appear in the character of a servant; and <div eID="gen42527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42528" type="x-p"/> 2. that he might have it in readiness to dry their feet after he had washed them.
entries.5af0af2aad54220f3b9fc9c34856f677b9ea1784: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen42528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42529" type="x-p"/> Poureth water into a bason, etc. - This was the office of the meanest slaves. When David sent to Abigail, to inform her that he had chosen her for wife, she arose and said: Behold, let thy handmaid be a Servant, to Wash the Feet of the Servants of my lord, <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.41">1Sam 25:41</reference>. Some of the ancients have supposed that our Lord began with washing the feet of Judas, to inspire him with sentiments of compunction and remorse, to melt him down with kindness, and to show all his disciples how they should act towards their enemies. Dr. Lightfoot supposes he washed the feet of Peter, James, and John only; but this is not likely: the verb αρχεσθαι in the sacred writings, signifies, not only to commence, but to finish an act, <reference osisRef="Act.1.1">Act 1:1</reference>; and in the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.3">Gen 2:3</reference>. There is every reason to believe that he washed the feet of all the twelve. See on <reference osisRef="Joh.13.9">Joh 13:9</reference> (note).
entries.2afba7262afb426a765ace3314c8ae71fbf9dc23: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen42529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42530" type="x-p"/> Lord, dost Thou wash My feet? - Every word here is exceedingly emphatic. Peter had often seen the great humility of his Lord, but never saw his condescension so particularly marked as in this instance.
entries.7cdaee60442821d0ac86c2c6d747a01843e123be: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen42530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42531" type="x-p"/> What I do thou knowest not now, etc. - As if our Lord had said, Permit me to do it now, and I will shortly explain to you the nature of this action, and my motives for doing it. <div eID="gen42531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42532" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt know hereafter - Μετα ταυτα, after this business is finished. And so we find he explained the whole to them, as soon as he had finished the washing: see <reference osisRef="Joh.13.12-Joh.13.17">Joh 13:12-17</reference>. I cannot think that this refers to any particular instruction received on this head after the day of pentecost, as some have conjectured.
entries.7d7882b65f4719c781e8a153f864e6cf766ce796: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen42532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42533" type="x-p"/> If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me - Thou canst not be my disciple unless I wash thee. It is certain Christ did not mean to exclude him from the apostolic office, if he should persist, through the deepest reverence for his Master, to refuse to let him wash his feet: this act of his was emblematical of something spiritual; of something that concerned the salvation of Peter; and without which washing he could neither be an apostle or be finally saved; therefore our Lord said, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me. There is a mystical washing by the blood of Christ, <reference osisRef="1Jn.1.7">1Jn 1:7</reference>; and by his Spirit, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Cor 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Tit.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Tit.3.6">Tit 3:6</reference>. It was the common custom of our Lord to pass from sensible and temporal things to those which were spiritual and eternal; and to take occasion from every thing that presented itself, to instruct his disciples, and to raise their souls to God. If the discourse was of bread, water, leaven, father, mother, riches, etc., he immediately changed the literal sense, and under the figure of these things, spoke of matters altogether spiritual and Divine. I have met with many good persons who have attempted to imitate our blessed Lord in this, but I never knew one to succeed in it. The reason is, it requires not only very deep piety, but sound sense, together with an accurate knowledge of the nature and properties of the subjects which, in this way, the person wishes to illustrate; and very few can be found who have such deep, philosophical knowledge as such cases require. The large folio which a good-intentioned man printed on the metaphors is, alas! a standing proof how little mere piety can do in matters of this kind, where the sciences, and especially practical philosophy, are totally wanting. Jesus Christ was a consummate philosopher: every subject appears grand and noble in his hands. See an ample proof in the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="Joh.12.24">Joh 12:24</reference> (note).
entries.799dc5d8cb6611b48338a2d664fde1a0b956e983: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen42533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42534" type="x-p"/> Lord, not my feet only, etc. - It appears that Peter entered into our Lord's meaning, and saw that this was emblematical of a spiritual cleansing: therefore he wishes to be completely washed.
entries.989a76fa4e7b0c0b820ef09033aed80eab115dd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen42534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42535" type="x-p"/> He that is washed - That is, he who has been in the bath, as probably all the apostles had lately been, in order to prepare themselves the better for the paschal solemnity; for on that occasion, it was the custom of the Jews to bathe twice. <div eID="gen42535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42536" type="x-p"/> Needeth not save to wash his feet - To cleanse them from any dirt or dust that might have adhered to them, in consequence of walking from the bath to the place of supper. The washing, therefore, of the feet of such persons was all that was necessary, previously to their sitting down to table; The Hindoos walk home from bathing barefoot, and, on entering the house wash their feet again. To this custom our Lord evidently alludes. <div eID="gen42536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42537" type="x-p"/> If these last words of our Lord had any spiritual reference, it is not easy to say what it was. A common opinion is the following: He who is washed - who is justified through the blood of the Lamb, needeth only to wash his feet - to regulate all his affections and desires; and to get, by faith, his conscience cleansed from any fresh guilt, which he may have contracted since his justification. <div eID="gen42537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42538" type="x-p"/> Ye are clean, but not all - Eleven of you are upright and sincere; the twelfth is a traitor. So it appears he had washed the feet of all the twelve; but as no external ablutions can purify a hypocrite or a traitor, therefore Judas still remained unclean.
entries.d1841ed6e08744ddf68cec58d0076f4e447554f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen42538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42539" type="x-p"/> Know ye what I have done - Our Lord had told Peter, in the presence of the rest, <reference osisRef="Joh.13.7">Joh 13:7</reference>, that he should afterwards know what was the intent and meaning of this washing; and now he begins to fulfill his promise; therefore I think it more likely that he gives a command, here, than asks a question, as he knew himself that they did not comprehend his design. On this account γινωσκετε might be translated in the imperative mood, Consider what I have done.
entries.414a4b4b2fbe18dbed627385e87459eee7280ca2: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen42539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42540" type="x-p"/> Ye call me Master and Lord - Ὁ διδασκαλος και ὁ κυριος, similar to רבי Rabbi, and מר Mar, titles very common among the Jewish doctors, as may be seen in Schoettgen. This double title was not given except to the most accredited teachers, רבי ומורי Rabbi vemore, my master, my lord!
entries.1576122eb3fffefe734b7d7e86f6aa0210034158: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen42540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42541" type="x-p"/> Ye also ought to wash one another feet - That is, ye should be ready, after my example, to condescend to all the weakness of your brethren; to be willing to do the meanest offices for them, and to prefer the least of them in honor to yourselves.
entries.116e3be38994dfaf93094dc0d18c03be7f92ac07: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen42541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42542" type="x-p"/> The servant is not greater than his lord - Christ has ennobled the acts of humility by practising them himself. The true glory of a Christian consists in being, in his measure, as humble as his Lord. <div eID="gen42542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42543" type="x-p"/> Neither he that is sent - Ουδε αποϚολος Nor an apostle. As I think these words were intended for the suppression of all worldly ambition and lordly conduct in the apostles and their successors in the ministry, therefore I think the original word αποϚολος, should be translated apostle, rather than he that is sent, because the former rendering ascertains and determines the meaning better.
entries.17f12810dd04d0110813127a10c62e51b9191567: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen42543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42544" type="x-p"/> If ye know these things, happy, etc. - True happiness consists in the knowledge of God, and in obedience to him. A man is not happy because he knows much; but because he receives much of the Divine nature, and is, in all his conduct, conformed to the Divine will. "They who have read many books (says Menu) are more exalted than such as have seldom studied; they who retain what they have read, than forgetful readers; they who fully understand, than such as only remember; and they who perform their known duty, than such as barely know it.
