               <ns0:p>NOw <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 26.2.</ns0:note> before the feast of the passover <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That this was the <ns0:hi>fourth Passover</ns0:hi> after that he entred upon his publick Ministry, is out of doubt, and the last he ever celebrated. We have taken notice of this Evangelist's mention of the other three: but how long what follows was before the Passover, which is here exprest by [<ns0:hi>Before the Feast</ns0:hi>] is a great question: Some will have it <ns0:hi>the day,</ns0:hi> others <ns0:hi>immediately</ns0:hi> before, as <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> (the very same particle) is used, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 11.38. <ns0:hi>before dinner,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.15. <ns0:hi>be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore</ns0:hi> I <ns0:hi>suffer.</ns0:hi> The resolution of it much dependeth upon another question as difficult, <ns0:hi>viz. What Supper it is which is mentioned?</ns0:hi> Ver. 2. Those who would be satisfied in these cases, may find a collection of what is said by most valua<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble Interpreters in Mr. <ns0:hi>Pools Synopsis Criticorum,</ns0:hi> upon <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26. It is our happiness, that tho some such knots occur in holy Writ, yet they are about things in which our Salvation is not concerned; so as without danger to our Souls, we may be ignorant of what is the truth about them.</ns0:note>, when Jesus knew that his hour was come, that he should depart out of this world unto the Father <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">When Christ knew that the hour (which he had once or twice before said was <ns0:hi>not come</ns0:hi>) was now come, that he must die, rise again, and in a short time ascend to his Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther;</ns0:note>, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He having loved his Disciples, not with a muta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble but with an unchangeable love; he resolveth upon the washing of their feet, as a demonstration of that love.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And Supper being ended <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Possibly it were better translated, while they were at Supper, or in Supper time, <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, but the great question is, <ns0:hi>What Supper is here</ns0:hi> intended? Our most Learned <ns0:hi>Lightfoot</ns0:hi> is very confident, this was not the <ns0:hi>Pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chal Supper.</ns0:hi> The most Interpreters, Ancient and modern, seem to be of another mind; or it may be rather a common Supper which they ate before the Passover: for whereas some think this Supper was that in the House of <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> the Leper, mentioned <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.6. It seemeth no way probable, no circumstance inclining us to believe any such thing; and the Evangelist having told us that it was after that Supper, that Christ rode into <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and again went from thence, and hid himself, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.36. and then reporting this as a thing subsequent to it in this Chapter: It seemeth very clear to me, that it could not be the Supper in the House of <ns0:hi>Simon</ns0:hi> the Leper.</ns0:note>, the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">ver. 27.</ns0:note> devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot Simons <ns0:hi>son,</ns0:hi> to betray him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Concerning the influence of the Devil upon <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> to put it into his heart to betray his Master, see <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 Jesus knowing <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matt. 11.27. and 28 18. Chap. 3.35. chap. 17.2.</ns0:note> that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he was come from God, and went to God <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Our translating the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Participle <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>knowing,</ns0:hi> (which properly signifies <ns0:hi>having known</ns0:hi>) createth a diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culty, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> How Christs knowledge of this, that the Father had given all things into his hand, should be assigned as a reason of, or motive to his subsequent action of washing the feet of his Disciples? The sense therefore must certainly be, <ns0:hi>Tho he knew</ns0:hi>; and so it doth not import a reason of his following action, but onely signifieth Christs great humilia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion and condescention. Tho he well enough knew, that <ns0:hi>all power was given him in Heaven and Earth,</ns0:hi> as in <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 28.18. That he was his disciples Lord, that he came <ns0:hi>from God,</ns0:hi> and was now going to God again; yet to shew how much he loved his Disciples, and to set them a pattern of humility, and teach them brotherly love, and that he came not in the estate wherein he yet was to be ministred unto, but to minister, <ns0:hi>Matth</ns0:hi> 20.28.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 He riseth from supper, and layeth aside his gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments, and took a towel, and girded himself <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>He riseth from Supper,</ns0:hi> what Supper is the question; We are told, that the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had two Suppers upon the Pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chal night, which was the 14th. day of the month <ns0:hi>Nisan.</ns0:hi> The first, was the <ns0:hi>Passover Supper,</ns0:hi> which was a Religious rite in obedience to the Law. The second, a common Sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per, (as on other nights) to which our Saviour added a third, which was the <ns0:hi>Lords Supper.</ns0:hi> To me it seemeth ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther that their common Supper was first, then the Passo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver Supper; and that Christ arose from this common Sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per, to do this act. <ns0:hi>Augustine</ns0:hi> understood it of the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon Supper; so doth <ns0:hi>Beza, Heinsius, Tarnovius,</ns0:hi> and others which seemeth to me most probable; tho others understand it of the Passover Supper. Whatever Supper the Evangelist meaneth, Christ rose up from it before it was done. <ns0:hi>Calvin, Pareus, Beza, Petargus, Tossanus,</ns0:hi> and divers others amongst the Protestant Interpreters; <ns0:hi>Tolet, Maldonate,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iansenius,</ns0:hi> amongst the <ns0:hi>Papists,</ns0:hi> do agree a common Supper this night, beside the <ns0:hi>Paschal</ns0:hi> Supper, and the Lords Supper; from which it is most probable that Christ, as is here said, rose up, and laid aside his garment, that is, his outward loose garment, (for such they used) which servants were wont to gird up when they waited at Table, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 17.8. Christ laid one aside, and girded up the other, takes a towel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 After that, he poureth water into a ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, and began to wash the disciples feet, and to wipe <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> with the towel wherewith he was girded <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Poureth water into a bason; beginneth first to wash his Disciples feet, then to wipe them with the linnen cloth he had taken: All this was done in the form of a servant, (so they used to do, as to guests that came to Dine or Sup with their Lords or Masters.)</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 Then cometh he to Simon <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">Gr. He.</ns0:note> Peter: And Peter saith unto him, Lord <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See Matth. 3.14.</ns0:note>, doest thou wash my feet <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Christ in the performance of this <ns0:hi>Ceremony</ns0:hi> cometh to <ns0:hi>Simon Peter</ns0:hi>; whether first, or last, it is not said; (and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> argue all from hence, to prove the primacy of <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> over the rest of the Apostles) <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> looks upon it with a modest, but sinful and superstitious indignation. <ns0:hi>Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />muel</ns0:hi> of old determined, that <ns0:hi>Obedience to God is better than Sacrifice</ns0:hi>; it is then certainly better than a <ns0:hi>Comple<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment. Peter</ns0:hi> in this case ought not to have contradicted his Master out of a complement to him, but to have suffered him to go on in this act of Ministration. There may be a <ns0:hi>voluntary Humility,</ns0:hi> and pretended reverence to Christ, which is indeed but superstition, and can be no other if con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trary to any Revelation of the Divine Will.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Jesus answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now: but thou shalt know hereafter <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Our Lord, seeing <ns0:hi>Peters</ns0:hi> general design good, tho <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>he mistook as to this particular Act; tells him, that at pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent he did not understand his Counsel and design in this Action, but it should be more intelligible unto him after<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards, as indeed he made it by his discourse upon this his Act of humiliation, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 13, 14, 15, 16.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 3.5. 1 Cor. 6 11. Eph. 5.26. Titus 3.5. Heb 10.22.</ns0:note>, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> rashly replies, <ns0:hi>Thou shalt never wash my feet.</ns0:hi> Here was a seeming <ns0:hi>Reverence</ns0:hi> for his Master, but (like the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> zeal mentioned by <ns0:hi>Paul, Rom.</ns0:hi> 10.2.) <ns0:hi>not according to knowledge</ns0:hi>; Christ tells him, that except <ns0:hi>he washed him,</ns0:hi> he had no part with him; that is, he should never be saved. But will some say, Was not this too severe for our Saviour to threaten <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> with an exclusion from a <ns0:hi>Coinheritance</ns0:hi> with him in Heaven, for modestly refusing to suffer him to wash his feet? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> The least disobedience not repented of, is enough to exclude a Soul from the Kingdom of Heaven. 2. But Christ seems to take an advantage here, from this ce<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />remony of his washing their feet, to discourse to him the ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessity of his <ns0:hi>washing</ns0:hi> his Soul with his blood, from the filth of sin and corruption; and of this washing, it undoubtedly is that Christ here speaketh, the necessity of which is very often inculcated in holy Writ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 Simon Peter saith unto him, Lord, not my feet onely, but also <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> hands and <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> head <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> now understande h what <ns0:hi>washing</ns0:hi> it is which our Saviour last spake of, and wholly submitteth to the Will of his Lord and Master; acknowledging himself to be wholly defiled, and to stand in need of a washing all over. Lord, saith he, not <ns0:hi>my feet onely,</ns0:hi> but my <ns0:hi>hands</ns0:hi> and my <ns0:hi>head</ns0:hi> also, that is, my whole man.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Jesus saith to him, He that is washed, needeth not, save to wash <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> feet <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Look as it is with persons that have been washing them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves in a Bath, when they are washed, yet walking abroad bare-foot, or with thin Sandals, or coverings for their feet, will be again subject to pollute and dirty their feet; so as they will have frequent need to wash them again; but they need not soon again wash their whole bodies: so it is as to Souls that are washed with my blood, <ns0:hi>washed, and sanctified, ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stified in the Name of the Lord Iesus, and by the Spirit of God</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> (as the Apostle speaketh, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6.11.) their <ns0:hi>state</ns0:hi> is not to be renewed; they need not be justified a second time, but they will have need to have their feet washed in regard of their remainder of sin, and lust that is in them, and will be so while they are in the World, and the tempta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions which every where lie in the World, as snares for their feet; they will have need of a daily washing by repentance, and fresh applications of their Souls to my blood, by the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peated exercises of faith, according to their renewed and repeated acts of sin.</ns0:note>, but is clean every whit: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15.3.</ns0:note> ye are clean, but not all <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">You, who are my Apostles, are clean, you are washed, you are justified; I have forgiven your sins, accepted your persons, <ns0:hi>but not all</ns0:hi>; the most of you are so, but not all.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:358" />11 For he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.64.</ns0:note> knew who should betray him, therefore said he, Ye are not all clean <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">By these words, the Evangelist expounds onely what our Saviour meant in the former verse, when he had told them, they were not <ns0:hi>all clean</ns0:hi>; for tho the Disciples did not yet know that they had a <ns0:hi>Traytor</ns0:hi> amongst them, <ns0:hi>Satan</ns0:hi> had before this, put the design into the heart of <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> ver. 2. and Christ who knew all hearts, knew what was in the heart of <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> and he soon after (as we shall hereafter in this Chapter read) revealed it; yet at this time he had not revealed it to his Disciples: Now he begins to discover it, tell<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing them, that tho the most of them were clean, justified, and sanctified, yet all of them were not so.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 So after he had washed their feet, and had taken his garments <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">After that our Saviour had finished this Ceremony, and washed his Disciples feet; (some question whether all or no, but I see no reason to doubt it)</ns0:note>, and was set down again <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">he returned again to the Supper, which (probably) now was near finished, which cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tainly was the common Supper which the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> had besides the <ns0:hi>Passover Supper,</ns0:hi> and probably before it, tho some think after it.</ns0:note>, he said unto them, Know ye what I have done to you <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He asketh them, if they knew the meaning of this which he had done unto them; lest they should not fully understand it, he openeth it to them in the following dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 23.8, 10. 1 Cor. 8.6. and 12, 18. Phil. 2.11.</ns0:note> Ye call me Master and Lord, and ye say well: for <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> I am <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The Disciples in their ordinary discourses, called Christ <ns0:hi>Master</ns0:hi> and Lord; nor was it a name improper for him, for he was their Master to instruct them, their Lord to rule, guide, and govern them;</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">now saith our Saviour, Disciples ought to obey their Master, Servants ought to obey their Lords, and Disciples also ought to imitate their Master.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 22.27.</ns0:note> If I then <ns0:hi>your</ns0:hi> Lord and Master have wash<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed your feet <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Gal. 6.1, 2.</ns0:note>, ye also ought to wash one anothers feet <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">I have by this my action taught you to love, and to be ready also to serve one another, and not to think much to serve them even in the lowest and meanest offices by which you can do them good; for we must not think, that these words lay a litteral obligation upon Christians, to <ns0:hi>wash the feet of others</ns0:hi>; washing the feet is mentioned but as <ns0:hi>Species pro genere,</ns0:hi> a single act of service, but for all other acts by which we can be serviceable unto others; so it is also used, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 25.41. and 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 5.10. Some of the Ancients seem to have judged this <ns0:hi>washing of feet,</ns0:hi> to have been instituted as a Sacrament, (tho in an improper sense) and from hence, (tho <ns0:hi>Bellarmine, Maldonate</ns0:hi> and others, deny it to be a Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crament as well as we) yet probably is the practice in use amongst the <ns0:hi>Papists,</ns0:hi> to wash certain persons feet every <ns0:hi>Thursday</ns0:hi> before <ns0:hi>Easter,</ns0:hi> (a theatrical Ceremony, rather than any thing of solid and profitable use.) Our Saviour certain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly intends no more by <ns0:hi>ye ought to wash one anothers feet,</ns0:hi> than ye ought to serve one another in all offices of love, and not to think your selves too good, or too great, to do the meanest services to those who are my Disciples; and this is that as to which he tells them, he had set them an example that they should do as he had done, in other acts of the same kind, tho not as to this specifical act.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Pet. 2.21. 1 John 2.6.</ns0:note> I have given you an example, that ye should do, as I have done to you.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Verily, verily I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his Lord, neither he that is sent, greater then he that sent him <ns0:note n="⸫" place="bottom">The Apostles were to take up a very high station in the Gospel Church, and our hearts are very prone to swell in an high opinion of our selves, for which the nature of man taketh advantage from every thing in which we either really do excel, or can conceit that we do excel our neigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bours: Our Lord therefore, tho speaking to the Apostles, (some of the best of men) yet knowing they were (like <ns0:hi>Elij<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>h</ns0:hi>) men subject to like passions with other men, addeth this to arm them against any <ns0:hi>Temptation</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Pride</ns0:hi>; they owned themselves as servants to Christ who was their great Lord; they had seen what he had done; he therefore applieth a pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verbial expression to them, which he also made use of in o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther cases, as <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10.24. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 15.20. in both which places he maketh use of it to arm them against persecutions; here to perswade them to humility, condescention, and bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />therly love.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">James 1.25.</ns0:note> If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">he tells them, that it is not the bare comprehen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion of these things in their Notion, that would do them any good, unless they brought their knowledge into practice; for <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 4.17. <ns0:hi>To him that knoweth to do good, and doth it not, it is sin.</ns0:hi> Faith without works is dead, and the <ns0:hi>Knowledge of our</ns0:hi> Masters will, (if we do it not) doth but expose us to many stripes.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">There</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 I speak not of you <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">I am about to tell you what will make your ears tingle; but be of good comfort, what I shall now tell you, doth not concern all of you, it concerneth but one man amongst you.</ns0:note> all, I know whom I have chosen <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">I know whom I have chosen to the work of the Apostle<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship: so some interpret it, as <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.70 <ns0:hi>Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a Devil?</ns0:hi> But the generality of the best Interpreters understand the choosing here mentio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned, of a <ns0:hi>choosing to Eternal Life,</ns0:hi> and perseverance in the way of God as a means in order to it, as <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.4. and so understood, here is a greater argument in this Text to prove the <ns0:hi>Godhead of Christ,</ns0:hi> as the Author of <ns0:hi>Eternal Election</ns0:hi>: tho one of you be a <ns0:hi>Devil,</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Traytor,</ns0:hi> yet I have chosen the rest of you to Eternal Life: and this is no more than was Prophecied of me, and fulfilled in <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> as a Type of me: the Scripture must have its accomplishment: that Scripture is now fulfilled in me.</ns0:note>: but that the scripture may be fulfilled <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 41.9. Matth. 26.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> He that eateth bread with me, hath lift up his heel against me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or from henceforth</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 14.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. and 16.1.</ns0:note> Now I tell you before it come, that when it is come to pass, ye may believe that I am <ns0:hi>he</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">What I now tell you should be so far from prejudicing your faith in me, that it ought rather to confirm and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crease your faith in me as the true <ns0:hi>Messias</ns0:hi>; when (the thing coming to pass) you shall understand that I know the hearts, counsels, and secret thoughts of men: and when you shall see the Scriptures have their accomplishment, and those things which were long ago Prophecied concerning the <ns0:hi>Messias,</ns0:hi> have their just accomplishment, and fulfilling in me as the person intended in those Ancient Revelations.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Math. 10.4<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Verily, verily I say unto you, He that receiveth whomsoever I send, receiveth me; and he that receiveth me, receiveth him that sent me <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">See the notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10.24. The words of which place are but here repeated: either to commend to them brotherly love, and offices of love, which he had before re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />commended to them under the notion of <ns0:hi>washing one ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers feet</ns0:hi>: Or else to comfort his Disciples who might think that this treacherous villany of <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> would make them o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dious to the whole World: No, saith our Saviour, you are my messengers, persons sent by me; I will provide for you, there shall be those who will <ns0:hi>receive you</ns0:hi>: and I declare to all the World to incourage them, That I shall take their recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving of you as kindly as if they received me, and it shall turn to the same account, and that is all one as if they had received my Father himself, for he sent me. Some think that by these words Christ aggravateth the sin of <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> as being committed against the Father as well as against Christ: and a most treacherous failure as to the duty of an <ns0:hi>Apostle,</ns0:hi> or one dignified so much as to be sent out by Christ.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Math. 26.21.</ns0:note> When Jesus had thus said, he was trou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bled in spirit <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">How, and in what sense trouble of Spirit could agree to Christ, was noted before, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.27. (see the notes on that Text) this seemeth to have been rather a trouble of <ns0:hi>grief,</ns0:hi> that one of his Apostles, one whom he had chosen, should commit so great a villany, than arising from fear of Death.</ns0:note>, and testified, and said, Verily, verily I say unto you, that <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Acts 1.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 1 John 2.19.</ns0:note> one of you shall be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tray me <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">For his next words are a further discovery of the person that should betray him: he had said before, that he should be betrayed, and that it should be by one that used to eat bread with him: but now he cometh closer, and tells them that it should be by one of them, that is one of the twelve; this was a closer discovery than he had as yet made.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Then the disciples looked one on another, doubting of whom he spake <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">It seemeth they had no suspicion of <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> but our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour telling them that it was one of them, they begin to look about one upon another, rather suspecting themselves than <ns0:hi>Iudas.</ns0:hi> There may be a great deal of villany, and the greatest villany in the hearts of Professors, in whose conver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sation appeareth nothing that may give a just suspition to others, and the true Disciples of Christ will have so much candor and brotherly love, that they will not rashly judge and censure their brethren.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:358" />23 Now there was leaning on Jesus bosom <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This <ns0:hi>leaning on Iesus his bosom,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>lying on Iesus his breast,</ns0:hi> mentioned <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 25. cannot be understood without the understanding of the usual posture the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> used at their meals, and particularly, at the Paschal Supper: of which we have spoken largely in our notes upon <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.20. (see the Annotations there) Their posture seemeth to have been kneeling, and resting their bodies back upon their legs, with a leaning upon their left elbow; and this seemeth not to have been so close, but that he that so sate, might use his other hand to take his meat; hence he who sate before any, sate with his back towards him, but leaning towards the bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />some of the other, which is here called a leaning on (that is towards) his bosome, and <ns0:hi>lying on his breast,</ns0:hi> for it can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not be understood of such a setting, or leaning, as to touch the others breast or bosome, for that would have hindred him upon whom the person so leaned, from any use of his right hand to take his meat or drink. It is apparent from hence, that at this Supper there was none but <ns0:hi>Christ and his twelve Disciples.</ns0:hi> Secondly, that they sate in this <ns0:hi>posture of leaning</ns0:hi>: These two things make it very probable, if not cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain, that the Supper here mentioned was either the Paschal Supper, or a common Supper, which immediately went be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore, or followed after the <ns0:hi>Passover Supper.</ns0:hi> For 1. we have no record of any other Supper, at which were onely Christ and the twelve Disciples, and 2. if we may believe the <ns0:hi>Iewish</ns0:hi> Writers, tho their ordinary posture at their com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon meals was <ns0:hi>Discubiture,</ns0:hi> that is, a kneeling on their knees, with a resting their bodies backward upon their legs; yet this posture of leaning was constantly added onely upon the Passover night, as a further testimony of their liberty; that they were not now servants, (as in the land of <ns0:hi>Egypt.</ns0:hi>)</ns0:note>, one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The person who sate next to our Saviour, with his back next our Saviours bosome was <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> often in Scripture dig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nified with the title of the beloved Disciple, and him whom Jesus loved, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 19.26. and 20.2. and 21.7, 20.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Simon Peter therefore beckned to him, that he should ask who it should be of whom he spake <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> knowing the particular affection that Christ had for <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> maketh a sign to him, to ask of Christ which of them he meant; when he said, <ns0:hi>One of you shall betray me.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 He then lying on Jesus breast, saith unto him, Lord, who is it <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> accordingly doth propound the question to Christ.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 Jesus answered, He it is to whom I shall give a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or morsel, or little part.</ns0:note> sop, when I have dipped it <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">We have the same, tho not mentioned (as spoken in particular to <ns0:hi>Iohn) Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.23. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.21. tho nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther of them mention Christs own dipping the Sop; but <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>He dipped his hand with him in the dish</ns0:hi>; and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>His hand was with him on the table.</ns0:hi> With<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />out question all the Evangelists speak of the same time; for it is not reasonable to think that this discovery should be made, and <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> gone out, and that afterward he should return again to eat the <ns0:hi>Passover.</ns0:hi> This maketh me very in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clinable to think, that tho the <ns0:hi>washing of the feet</ns0:hi> might be during the time of a common Supper, preceding the Passo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver; yet the Supper they were now at was the <ns0:hi>Passover Supper</ns0:hi>: where, 1. were none but he and the twelve Disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples. 2. It is plain they were in that leaning posture, not used at common meals, but on the Passover nights, (as Dr. <ns0:hi>Lightfoot</ns0:hi> tells us from their Writings.) 3. The discourse passed at the Table is the very same (tho not in words, yet in sense) with that mentioned by <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> at the <ns0:hi>Passover Supper.</ns0:hi> 4. It is not reasonable to think, that after such a discovery as Christ now made of the Traitor, he should come again to be pointed at, and exposed. Concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the <ns0:hi>Sop</ns0:hi> what it was, hath been some question; and a Learned Writer of our own, (but in this point I think much too critical) hath increased the difficulty, by affirming the word here used [<ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>] signifies a piece of bread, or the lower part or chippings of the bread; for which he quoteth <ns0:hi>Hesychius,</ns0:hi> who indeed doth say so of <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> but not <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. The Learned Annotator thinks, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> is a false Print for <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, but it cannot be: for 1. there are in <ns0:hi>Hesychius</ns0:hi> several words in Alphabetical order, between <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> and this word. 2. Tho <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> be not in <ns0:hi>Hesychius,</ns0:hi> yet <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> is, and expounded by him <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> parts; now all know that this <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which is but a diminutive derived from <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> or <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, can signifie no more, than a little part, let it be of what it will; for it is manifest out of <ns0:hi>Homer,</ns0:hi> that joined with an adjective, it signifies a mouth <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of mans Flesh, which came out of the <ns0:hi>Cyclops</ns0:hi> his mouth. So as the sense of these words is, He it is to whom I shall give a little part or portion of meat, when I have dipt it:</ns0:note>. And when he had dipped the sop, he gave it to Judas Iscariot the son of Simon <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">And having dipt it, he gave it to <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Son of Simon</ns0:hi>: not the <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> who wrote the Epistle, and who is mentioned, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 14.22. but he that was the son of <ns0:hi>Simon,</ns0:hi> called from his place which he lived in <ns0:hi>[Kiroth] Iscariot,</ns0:hi> by which he did as perfectly describe the <ns0:hi>Traytor,</ns0:hi> as if he had named him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 And after the sop Satan entred into him <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">That the Devil did ever so enter into <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> as to possess him, as we read of many who were possessed, and violently acted by the Devil, is more than we read any wherein holy Writ; the <ns0:hi>entrance into him,</ns0:hi> signifies <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> his free and willing giving up of himself to the Devils s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ggestions and conduct: and in this sense the Dev<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> also before this time was entred into <ns0:hi>Iudas, Luke</ns0:hi> 22.3. But as holy men are said to be filled with the Spirit of God, who had before received the Spirit, because the holy Spirit came after upon them with fuller and stronger impulses, and notions: so tho the Devil had formerly been moving <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> to this vile Act, and had had his consent to it; yet after he had taken this <ns0:hi>mouthfull,</ns0:hi> the Devil plyed him with stronger notions, impu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ses, and suggestions: and now he had master'd his conscience, and hardned his heart, so as he was more prepared for the <ns0:hi>Vil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lany</ns0:hi> about which he had some thoughts before: he had now with an unbelieving, and unthankful heart, been eating the <ns0:hi>Passover,</ns0:hi> which was a Type of Christ; and had so mastered his conscience, as to come and do this, with a vile heart, reaking before with treacherous and bloody designs against his Lord and Master: See what is the effect. His heart is more vile, more treacherous, and bloody, he is twice more the servant of the Devil than he was before. The sop given him by Christ, was but an accidental occasion of it; as the Devil took more advantage from his now hardned, and fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther imboldned heart, and he is twice more the child of the Devil than he was before.</ns0:note>. Then Jesus said unto him, That thou doest, do quickly <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Christ knowing this, doth not command, advise, or exhort him, but in a detestation, bids him go and do what he was resolved to do, and which he knew would be <ns0:hi>quickly</ns0:hi>; letting him both know, that he knew what was in his heart, and that he was now ready to receive the effects of his malice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 Now no man <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Of them tha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> were sat down.</ns0:note> at the table knew for what intent he spake this unto him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 For some <ns0:hi>of them</ns0:hi> thought, because Judas had the bag <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">How innocent are honest hearts? Charity thinketh no evil, (saith the Apostle) altho our Saviour had plainly enough deciphered him as the Traytor, by telling <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> that he to whom he should give the <ns0:hi>Sop,</ns0:hi> was he; and then by giving it to <ns0:hi>Iudas,</ns0:hi> yet whether they all did not hear what our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our said to <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> or did not think of so sudden a Tragedy; they do not suspect that the hour was at hand, when <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> should perfect his intended Villany; tho they heard our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour bid him get him out, and do quickly, what he had to do; yet <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> being he who carried</ns0:note>, that Jesus had said unto him, Buy <ns0:hi>those things</ns0:hi> that we have need of against the feast <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">that little stock of mony which Christ had, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 12.6. they thought that that which our Saviour bid him do, as a work he had undertaken to do, was laying out some monies, either to buy some things which were necessary for them, for the seven days of the Feast of unleavened bread; either for food for them to <ns0:hi>eat,</ns0:hi> or for <ns0:hi>Sacrifices</ns0:hi> for them to offer.</ns0:note>: or that he should give something to the poor <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or that it was our Saviours mind, that he should out of this little stock, distri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bute something to the poor; they little thought that our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viours words argued a giving him over to perfect the trea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cherous designs which he had conceived in his heart.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 He then having received the sop, went im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mediately out <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">From hence appeareth, 1. That it is impossible to prove that <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> was with our Saviour, when he Instituted and Celebrated the Supper; tho if he were, it proveth nothing of a liberty for ignorant and scandalous persons to be there; (for <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> was not such a one) nor yet of a lawfulness for Ministers of the Gospel, knowing any to be such, to give the Lords Supper to them. For altho Christ knew <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> his heart, yet he acted not according to his Omniscience<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but as the first and prime Minister of the Gospel, setting us an ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ample, not to judge of secret things, but of things open onely. 2. It also appeareth from hence, that it is not pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bable, that this was any other Supper than the <ns0:hi>Passover Sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per</ns0:hi>; for if it were not, the Passover Supper must be after this, and this same Supper preceding it. Our famous Dr. <ns0:hi>Lightfoot</ns0:hi> thinks it was a Supper in <ns0:hi>Bethany,</ns0:hi> at two miles distance (or near so much) from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> But then it must follow, 1. That <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> speaks nothing of the <ns0:hi>Paschal Supper,</ns0:hi> or the Lords Supper; and 2. it doth by no means appear probable to me, that <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> after such a discovery of him, should come again to eat the Passover with Christ and his Disciples. These things, together with what I noted be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore, that here is no mention made of more guests than the twelve; that the posture used (especially as to leaning) was peculiar to the <ns0:hi>Paschal Supper.</ns0:hi> That the discourse mentio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned by this Evangelist, as had at this Supper about the disco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />very of the Traytor, is the same in substance, (tho not in terms) with what <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> report, as passed at the <ns0:hi>Passover.</ns0:hi> All these things confirm me, that it is the Paschal Supper that <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> speaketh of; whether <ns0:hi>Iudas</ns0:hi> was at the <ns0:hi>Lords Supper,</ns0:hi> which we know followed the Passover imme<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diately, depends upon the sense of the particle <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, which we translate <ns0:hi>immed<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>tely</ns0:hi>; but doth not signifie necessarily such a present departure; but the action of the Lords Supper might be first over, tho in reason it seemeth to me more prob<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>b<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     </ns0:gap>e, because of those words, <ns0:hi>having received the sop, he immediately went out:</ns0:hi> that it should be here Interpreted strictly, and that shame and horror should not suffer him to stay so long, as till the action of the Supper was over: tho whether he were at the Lords Supper (as I said before) sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fieth nothing at all to the questions about <ns0:hi>mixt Communion,</ns0:hi> either as to the part of the Minister administring, or the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples Communicating.</ns0:note>: And it was night <ns0:hi>u.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:359" />31 Therefore when he was gone out, Jesus said, Now is the son of man glorified <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">He speaketh of that which was presently to be, as if it were already done; the meaning is, Now the time cometh when the Son of man shall immediately be glorified, by fini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shing the work which God hath given him to do, by rising again from the dead, and declaring himself to be the Son of God with Power, by Ascending up into Heaven, to be glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rified with the same glory which he had with the Father be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the World began:</ns0:note>, and God is glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rified in him <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">And God will appear to be glorifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in him, by his finishing the work which God hath given him to do, manifesting his name to the sons of men; and by the many signs and wonders which God will yet further shew at the time of his Death and Resurrection, and by the coming down of the Holy Ghost.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 17.1, 5, 6.</ns0:note> If God be glorified in him, God shall also glorifie him in himself, <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">God was glorified in Christ by his Death upon the Cross in obedience to his Fathers Will; thus <ns0:hi>Peter Chap.</ns0:hi> 21.19. is said by his Death to <ns0:hi>glorifie God</ns0:hi>; and as he was declared to be the Son of God, and as by him the World was brought to the knowledge of God, as by his Spiritual and Heavenly Doctrine, so by the miracles he wrought. From hence our Lord concludeth, that God should glorifie Christ in himself, so as the glory of the Father and the Son are the same, they are mutually glorified each in other: If the Son be glorified, the Father is also glorified; and if the Father be glorified, the Son is also glorified; the Father and the Son are mutually glorified each in other.</ns0:note> and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">chap. 12.23.</ns0:note> shall straightway glorifie him <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And the Father (saith our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our) in a short time will further glorifie him, by taking him up into Heaven, and making the whole person of the Media<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tor glorious in Heaven</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 Little children, yet a little while I am with you <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Our Saviours time of Death being very nigh, (for it was the next day) he beginneth to speak of it to his Disciples more freely, and plainly, and to let them know, that he, tho now dying, bare a fatherly tender affection to them, he calls them <ns0:hi>little Children</ns0:hi>; Parents have a natural affection to their Children, a more tender affection to their Children when little, because in their tender age they are more ignorant, and unable to provide for themselves. We find this compel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation used by Christs Apostles, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.19. and 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.1, 28. and he tells them, that he had but now a little time to be with them before his Death, and not long after his Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />surrection; in which too, his converse was not such with them, as it hitherto had been.</ns0:note>, ye shall seek me: and, as I said to the Jews, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 8.21.</ns0:note> whether I go ye cannot come; so now I say to you <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He told this to the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 7.34. and now he tells them the same, that they would miss him when he was gone, and should seek him; but even the Disciples at present could not follow him to Heaven whi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther he was going: The unbelieving <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> should never fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />low him thither, but even those who were his Disciples, who were born again, and whom he loved as little Children are beloved by their parents, should not yet follow him; his work in the World was done, but they had yet a great deal of work in it to do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Cha 15.12, 19. 1 Thes 4.9. 1 John 3.23.</ns0:note> A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                  <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Commandment of loving one another, is strictly no new Commandment, we find it in the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses, Levit.</ns0:hi> 19.18. often pressed in the New Testament, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 15.17. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5.2. 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 4.21. St. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> in his first Epistle saith, it is no new Commandment, 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.7. 2 <ns0:hi>Epist</ns0:hi> 6. It is there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore called a new Commandment, either because of the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cellency of it; as new seemeth to be taken. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 33.3. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 65.17. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.29. or because it is expounded in the Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel in a new manner, pressed more plainly, and in new Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guments, and urged by a new example of their Lord and Master.</ns0:note> as I have loved you, that ye also love one another <ns0:hi>d.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 John 2.5. and 4 20.</ns0:note> By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, If ye have love one to another <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">A Disciple hath his name either from learning from his Master, or from following his Master, and treading in his steps; take it in either sense: Loving one another is a certain note of being Christs Disciples; for as Christ continually pres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sed this by his precepts, so he set them his own example, by shewing the greatest love to them he could shew.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 Simon Peter said unto him, Lord, whither goest thou? Jesus answered him, Whither I go, thou canst not follow me now <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 21 <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 2 Pet. 1.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note>: but thou shalt follow me afterwards <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> yet understood not his Lord and Master, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore asked him whither he went? Our Saviour spake of his Ascension into Heaven, after his suffering death upon the Cross; whither he tells <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> he could not at present fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />low him, but afterwards should. Believers shall be ever with the Lord, but they must wait the Lords time, and first finish the work which he hath given them to do upon the Earth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 Peter said unto him, Lord, why cannot I follow thee now <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Still <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> doth not understand our Saviour, but fanci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth some Earthly motion from the place where he was; but it should seem by what followeth, that he thought our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our spake of some motion which might be very dangerous to him.</ns0:note>? I will <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mar. 14.31. Luk. 22.33, 34.</ns0:note> lay down my life for thy sake <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">And therefore he adds, according to his usual cou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rage and mettal, expressed on all occasions, <ns0:hi>I will lay down my life for thy sake</ns0:hi>; we had such a resolution of his <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.33, 35.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 Jesus answered him, Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>before the cock crow twice.</ns0:hi> So the other three Evangelists must be expounded, who say no more than <ns0:hi>before the cock crow,</ns0:hi> not mentioning how often; but the hi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />story makes it good, that our Saviour meant thrice, for it was not before the second crowing of the Cock, that <ns0:hi>Peter went out, and wept bitterly.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
